title: Ravens Week 4 film study: Vega Ioane could be a long-term center
summary: The Ravens’ gritty Week 4 win over the Titans gave us another opportunity to evaluate several players in the trenches on both sides of the football. Mike Green stepped into a larger role as Baltimore’s primary edge rusher on passing downs, Nnamdi Madubuike continued to show that he has returned to form, and rookie first-round […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - OCTOBER 04: Olaivavega Ioane #71 of the Baltimore Ravens prepares to snap the ball before a play during the second half against the Tennessee Titans at M&T Bank Stadium on October 4, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Ravens’ gritty Week 4 win over the Titans gave us another opportunity to evaluate several players in the trenches on both sides of the football. Mike Green stepped into a larger role as Baltimore’s primary edge rusher on passing downs, Nnamdi Madubuike continued to show that he has returned to form, and rookie first-round pick Vega Ioane provided some much-needed stability along the interior offensive line in his first start at center. OLB Mike Green 40 snaps | 26 pass rush | 13 run defense | 1 coverage | 5 pressures With Trey Hendrickson out, Mike Green was expected to take on a larger role as a pass rusher, and he delivered. Green finished with five pressures while posting a 29.4% win rate on true pass sets, but one of the more interesting developments was the power he flashed throughout the game. On one rep, Green held a firm edge before using a rip move to work around the offensive tackle and make the tackle. On another, he struck the tackle with heavy hands, stood him up at the point of attack and worked off the block to make the play. Those reps were encouraging because Green’s game has largely been built around his quickness, hand usage and ability to win around the edge. Mike Green had 5 pressures, 3 qb hits and a 29.4 % win rate on true pass sets vs the Titans One interesting development has been his power usage, he’s trying to convert speed to power multiple times. He’s also a little more sawed off vs the run, synching into the ground. pic.twitter.com/3ErPw6k43W — Yuri (@Yuri_Ravens) October 5, 2026 As a pass rusher, Green continued to flash the cross chop that has become one of his most dependable moves. The timing of that move has gotten close to automatic, but he also showed some development within his pass-rush plan. On one rep, Green used a hesitation into a cross chop to open the offensive tackle’s hips before countering with an inside spin and generating pressure on the quarterback. On another, he converted speed to power, got inside the tackle’s chest and drove him backward into the quarterback’s lap. The encouraging part of Green’s performance was the variety. We already knew he could win with quickness and his cross chop, but adding legitimate power and counters gives tackles more to think about when trying to protect against him. As the season progresses, Green becoming a dependable pass-rush option will be important if the Ravens want to consistently generate pressure without Trey Hendrickson on the field. DT Nnamdi Madubuike 46 snaps | 16 run defense | 30 pass rush | 6 pressures Nnamdi Madubuike has started to pick things up over the last few weeks, and considering where he was physically a year ago, his return to form has been impressive. For a player who was facing the possibility of medical retirement, Madubuike looks as strong and explosive as he has at any point in his career. He finished the game with six pressures and recorded a 20% win rate on true pass sets. His ability to convert speed to power remains one of the most dangerous parts of his game. Madubuike has the athleticism to threaten offensive linemen off the snap before turning that momentum into power and collapsing the interior of the pocket. Nnamdi Madubuike lead the Ravens with 6 pressures vs the titans. He’s also had a 20% win rate on true pass sets and 2 QB hits The power and explosiveness are the best it has ever been, does not look like a guy who was about to medically retire. His upper body/ hand usage and… pic.twitter.com/LEzGWIye85 — Yuri (@Yuri_Ravens) October 5, 2026 That strength also showed up against the run. One of the more important aspects of Madubuike’s game has always been his ability to handle combination blocks, engage double teams and find ways to split offensive linemen. On one rep, he established inside leverage against the blocker before working his way into the backfield and helping force the running back into a minimal gain. Madubuike’s return has been great to see, but more importantly, his presence changes what Baltimore can do up front. Interior pressure forces quarterbacks off their spot and prevents them from simply stepping up when Baltimore’s edge rushers win around the corner. If Madubuike continues playing at this level, he will be a major piece of the Ravens developing a more consistent pass rush as the season progresses. C Vega Ioane 64 snaps | 30 run blocking | 34 pass blocking | 0 pressures allowed Vega Ioane made his first start at center this season, and there was a lot to like about what he showed. Ioane played all 64 offensive snaps and did not allow a pressure despite matching up with Jeffery Simmons multiple times throughout the game. One of Ioane’s biggest strengths is his ability to operate in close quarters. He does a good job preventing defensive linemen from getting clean access to his chest, while his punch timing and hand fighting allow him to maintain leverage and keep defenders at length. That showed up repeatedly against Simmons, where Ioane was able to absorb contact without surrendering significant ground in pass protection. His ability to quickly flip his hips also translates well to center. Ioane has the core strength to absorb power while maintaining his balance, and his movement skills allow him to redirect defenders once he establishes contact. Vega Ioane first career start at center 0 pressures allowed on 34 pass block snaps Smooth hips and initial punch, strong core and pass protection chops pic.twitter.com/hSaql2VVml — Yuri (@Yuri_Ravens) October 6, 2026 One rep in particular highlighted the combination of technique and athleticism that makes Ioane intriguing inside. Ioane used a snatch technique to throw the defensive lineman to the ground before immediately working downfield on a screen. It was a good example of his ability to win the initial engagement and then transition into his next assignment. The biggest takeaway from Ioane’s first start at center was stability. Baltimore’s interior offensive line has desperately needed reliable play, and allowing zero pressures over 34 pass-blocking snaps against a defensive front featuring Jeffery Simmons is an encouraging start. If Ioane can continue providing that level of pass protection while developing the finer details of playing center, the Ravens may have found an answer at a position that entered the season with plenty of uncertainty. Snap distribution and advanced metrics via Pro Football Focus.

title: AFC North Week 4 recap: Browns take the lead
summary: An unfamiliar face sits atop the competitive AFC North after four weeks of the season. Here are the latest updates from around the division: Cleveland Browns (3-1) The Cleveland Browns won their third consecutive game with a 27-24 victory over the Pittsburgh Steelers, taking the lead in the division in the process due to tiebreakers. […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - OCTOBER 1: Denzel Boston #12 of the Cleveland Browns reacts after completing a catch against the Pittsburgh Steelers during an NFL football game at Huntington Bank Field on October 1, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images An unfamiliar face sits atop the competitive AFC North after four weeks of the season. Here are the latest updates from around the division: Cleveland Browns (3-1) The Cleveland Browns won their third consecutive game with a 27-24 victory over the Pittsburgh Steelers, taking the lead in the division in the process due to tiebreakers. Deshaun Watson’s resurgence on the field continued into Week 4 as he led the Browns’ offense to set up a career-long 56-yard field goal from Andre Szmyt to take the lead with 10 seconds remaining in regulation. Watson finished the game 24 of 33 for 268 yards, a touchdown, and an interception while also losing a fumble. The story of the game for Cleveland’s offense, however, was the play of their two rookie wide receivers. Second-rounder Denzel Boston led the team with 89 yards on four catches while first-rounder KC Concepcion was second with 64 yards on five catches. Harold Fannin Jr. caught Watson’s lone touchdown. Quinshon Judkins led the team in rushing, but found little success with just 53 yards on 17 carries. The second-year back did find his way into the end zone once, though. The Browns’ defense made life difficult for Aaron Rodgers, sacking him five times while coming down with two interceptions against the future Hall-of-Fame quarterback. Denzel Ward snagged the first interception in the second quarter, while the second came from Grant Delpit on the final play of the game. Cleveland lost Mason Graham early in the game with what was later revealed to be a sprained MCL and ankle. The timeline for the 2025 fifth-overall pick is currently unknown. Baltimore Ravens (3-1) The Ravens improved to 3-1 with a 24-18 home win over the Tennessee Titans, but an ankle injury to Lamar Jackson overshadowed the victory. Jackson was stellar in the first half, completing 15 of 20 passes for 222 yards and two touchdowns before an ankle injury on a sack sidelined him for the remainder of the game. The NFL world now awaits clarity on the status of Jackson’s injury and how much time, if any, he may miss. Tyler Huntley replaced Jackson for the second half as the offense came to a screeching halt. Zay Flowers was on his way to another dominant outing before Jackson exited the game, finishing the day with a team-high 118 receiving yards and a touchdown on eight catches. Mark Andrews caught Jackson’s other touchdown as he found the end zone for the first time this season. Derrick Henry struggled to find running room against his old team, racking up 73 yards and a touchdown on 23 carries for just 3.2 yards per carry. Alongside Jackson, Baltimore also lost Durham Smythe to a torn Achilles, Andrew Vorhees to a foot injury, and Marlon Humphrey to a calf injury during the game. The Ravens’ defense has been under heavy scrutiny to start the season, and that was not helped by an up-and-down performance against a weak Titans’ offense. The game started strong with a Trenton Simpson interception on the first drive, but many of the same issues popped up throughout the game, including an inability to finish sacks and missed tackles. Undrafted rookie Ethan Burke recorded the team’s lone sack on Cam Ward. Kyle Hamilton forced a fumble on rookie first-rounder Carnell Tate, which was recovered by Malaki Starks. Starks also recovered an onside kick to ice the game. Pittsburgh Steelers (2-2) The Steelers dropped to 2-2 with a 27-24 loss on the road to the Browns. Pittsburgh rallied from a 21-10 hole at halftime, falling three points short in the end. Rodgers completed 22 of 40 passes for 299 yards and three touchdowns with two interceptions, although the second came with just 10 seconds remaining in the game. DK Metcalf had by far his best game of the season with five catches for 115 yards. Roman Wilson, Darnell Washington, and Pat Freiermuth were the recipients of Rodgers’ three touchdowns. Jaylen Warren had another strong performance with 93 rushing yards on 17 carries to go with three catches for 33 yards. The Steelers’ defense forced two turnovers on the night, a fumble forced and recovered by T.J. Watt, and an interception by Robert Spears-Jennings. Watt and Payton Wilson had the team’s two sacks on Watson. Pittsburgh lost Derrick Harmon during the game to a foot injury and Jamel Dean to an ankle injury. Harmon has since been placed on injured reserve, meaning he will miss at least four games. Dean is not expected to join Harmon on injured reserve. Cincinnati Bengals (2-2) After starting the season 2-0, the Bengals have now dropped back-to-back games following a 22-17 home loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars. Joe Burrow had a tough outing while losing his top two wide receivers during the game. Burrow finished 39 of 54 for 428 yards, a touchdown, and two picks. Tee Higgins had a team-high 157 receiving yards on 11 catches before a groin injury knocked him out of the game in the fourth quarter. Ja’Marr Chase left the game much earlier with a concussion, leaving Burrow possibly without his top two weapons next week against the Miami Dolphins. Cincinnati had next to nothing in the run game, with Chase Brown leading the team with just 10 yards on nine carries. The Bengals finished the game with only 23 total rushing yards. Cincinnati’s defense sacked Trevor Lawrence four times, with Dexter Lawrence, Boye Mafe, Myles Murphy, and Kris Jenkins Jr. all getting a sack.

Immediately after beating the Titans on Sunday afternoon, the Ravens were favored for next weekend’s trip to Atlanta. The Falcons’ 45-24 victory over the New Orleans Saints on Monday Night Football tightened the gap, and Tuesday morning’s negative update flipped the line entirely. The Ravens are now three-point underdogs ( via FanDuel Sportsbook ) for the first time this season. That line indicates surprising confidence in a Ravens team that was outscored 14-0 by the Titans without Jackson in the second half. Huntley has mounted gutsy wins before, but can he do so behind a battered offensive line (and without top blocking tight end Durham Smythe), against Atlanta’s elite run defense? Then there’s the Falcons’ explosive offense, which moved the ball at will against the Saints on Monday night. Bijan Robinson has been unstoppable so far this year – for that matter, so was Brian Robinson Jr. in New Orleans. The Ravens could be down multiple starting defenders in Week 5, too. Cornerback Marlon Humphrey left Sunday’s game with a calf injury, while edge rusher Trey Hendrickson could need more time to recover from finger surgery. All told, this is shaping up to be a tough matchup for the Ravens. At this point in the season, getting out of Atlanta healthy might be a win on its own, regardless of the outcome. title: Ravens QB Lamar Jackson has ‘only an outside chance’ to play in Week 5
summary: Score one for the social media injury experts who said that Baltimore Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson likely suffered a sprained ankle in Sunday’s win over the Tennessee Titans. That is indeed the diagnosis for the two-time MVP, who has “only an outside chance” to take the field in Week 5 against the Atlanta Falcons, per […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - OCTOBER 04: Lamar Jackson #8 of the Baltimore Ravens looks on from the sideline during the second half against the Tennessee Titans at M&T Bank Stadium on October 4, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images) | Getty Images Score one for the social media injury experts who said that Baltimore Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson likely suffered a sprained ankle in Sunday’s win over the Tennessee Titans. That is indeed the diagnosis for the two-time MVP, who has “only an outside chance” to take the field in Week 5 against the Atlanta Falcons, per NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport . A multi-game absence is possible. Ravens head coach Jesse Minter declined to provide any details on Jackson’s injury on Sunday or Monday, saying only that it would not be “crazy long-term,” which Rapoport also confirms. Minter will likely refer to the team’s upcoming injury reports when asked about Jackson’s status after practice on Wednesday. Tuesday’s update indicates that Jackson is unlikely to practice this week. Baltimore will want backup Tyler ‘Snoop’ Huntley to take reps with the first-team in preparation for a Falcons defense that has impressed through four weeks. Atlanta ranks close to the middle of the league in points allowed, but they have allowed the eighth-fewest yards with the league’s No. 1 run defense by a wide margin. That is especially problematic for a Ravens offense that leans on their ground game when Jackson is sidelined. The team’s O-line woes have already resulted in a drop in Derrick Henry’s production, which will be worsened by Jackson’s absence. Opposing offense have been able to move the ball through the air against the Falcons, though not very efficiently. If Sunday’s game comes down to Huntley making throws against a talented, well-coached secondary, the Ravens could be in serious trouble. Moving to 3-2 via a loss to an NFC team is by no means a season-threatening outcome, especially if the rest speeds Jackson’s recovery. Missing Week 6 against the 3-1 Browns would not be ideal, either, but perhaps withstandable. But the Ravens will need their superstar quarterback back on the field by the end of October when they face the Bengals, Bills, and Jaguars in successive weeks. title: Ravens TE Durham Smythe suffers season-ending torn Achilles
summary: Baltimore Ravens’ tight end Durham Smythe limped off the field Sunday’s win over the Tennessee Titans and was quickly ruled out with an Achilles injury. The sight of Smythe grabbing at his calf and struggled to walk under his own power sparked concerns about a potential tear. Unfortunately, those fears have proven to be accurate. […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - OCTOBER 04: Durham Smythe #80 of the Baltimore Ravens reacts to an injury during the third quarter of the game against the Tennessee Titans at M&T Bank Stadium on October 04, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Patrick Smith/Getty Images) | Getty Images Baltimore Ravens’ tight end Durham Smythe limped off the field Sunday’s win over the Tennessee Titans and was quickly ruled out with an Achilles injury. The sight of Smythe grabbing at his calf and struggled to walk under his own power sparked concerns about a potential tear. Unfortunately, those fears have proven to be accurate. According to NFL insider Ian Rapoport, MRI results confirmed that Smythe tore his Achilles and will miss the remainder of the season. #Ravens TE Durham Smythe suffered a torn Achilles on Sunday and he’s out for the season, the MRI confirmed. Unfortunately, exactly what it appeared Sunday. pic.twitter.com/yDHQ4IJXUz — Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) October 6, 2026 Smythe, 31, was signed to a one-year deal this offseason to fill a depth tight end role after the Ravens lost multiple players at the position in free agency. Smythe came from Chicago and was a natural fit in Declan Doyle’s offense given his experience in the system. The nine-year veteran had played over 100 offensive snaps for the Ravens this season prior to Week 4, serving as a versatile blocker. While Smythe was not a receiving factor for the Ravens, his blocking specialty and snap share will have to be backfilled. Rookie tight ends Matthew Hibner and Josh Cuevas are likely to take on bigger roles now behind Mark Andrews. Hibner and Cuevas have each flashed receiving upside through four games but will need to quickly mature as blockers in the run game and pass protection. The Ravens may look to acquire another free agent veteran or make a trade, as well, to further supplement the tight end room. Smythe was one of several injured players the Ravens lost in Week 4, which includes Lamar Jackson, Marlon Humphrey and Andrew Vorhees. This comes just a week after centers Jovaughn Gwyn and Ethan Pocic were placed on injured reserve, and Trey Hendrickson suffered a finger injury that kept him sidelined on Sunday. These mounting injuries will continue to challenge Jesse Minter’s roster in the coming weeks.

title: Buffalo Bills first quarter of season grades: Greg Rousseau and outside pass-rush rolling, secondary gets failing mark
summary: The Buffalo Bills are 3-1, and while that mark leaves them in first place in the AFC East, it feels like it could be—and should be—better. After winning their first three games, the Bills dropped a 29-26 decision to the New England Patriots on Sunday, breathing life into the Pats while making the AFC East […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - OCTOBER 4: Josh Allen #17 and Keon Coleman #0 of the Buffalo Bills celebrate during the fourth quarter against the New England Patriots at Highmark Stadium on October 4, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills are 3-1, and while that mark leaves them in first place in the AFC East, it feels like it could be—and should be—better. After winning their first three games, the Bills dropped a 29-26 decision to the New England Patriots on Sunday, breathing life into the Pats while making the AFC East standings a bit closer. Four games into the 2026 season, these Bills look like most of the Buffalo teams in the Josh Allen era: talented, flawed, and going as far as No. 17 can take them. Back in the old days, when the NFL played a 16-game regular-season schedule, the season divided neatly into four quarters. Now, with that seventeenth game in the fold, the math doesn’t quite math as easily. Fortunately for me, I teach English and not math, so the extra decimals after we divide 17 by 4 won’t bother me much. We also can’t call this portion of the season the “quarter pole,” as our friend Matt Warren has always been so passionately clear about. That horse racing term refers to the pole that is one-quarter mile away from the finish line, not from the starting line. This part of the season finds us much farther away from the end than the beginning. Our first quarter grades show a Buffalo team that has immense potential, but also that has one unit clearly lagging behind the others. _____________________________________________________________________________ Quarterbacks: B+ If I were to give a report card-style comment, my summation of Allen’s play so far would be this: “Performs inconsistently; work quality varies.” At times this season, Allen has been masterful. In the first two games of the season, he threw for 582 yards and five touchdowns with no turnovers. He had 92 rushing yards and four more touchdowns on the ground. He had a QB rating of 125.8 and he completed 66.7% of his passes. In Buffalo’s last two games, though, he’s not been nearly as effective. Allen is still completing passes at a high rate, completing 66.1% of his throws in the last two games. However, he’s passed for 457 yards with one touchdown against three interceptions. He’s rushed 13 times for just 26 yards, adding three more scores on the ground. His quarterback rating is just 73.9 over those two games, and he’s also lost a fumble. Allen shouldn’t need to be superhuman every week for Buffalo to compete, and while he played better against the Patriots than he did against the Los Angeles Chargers, he still wasn’t as good as he was in Weeks One and Two. Running Backs: B+ This is not a James Cook III message, as his individual grade is really what boosts this entire grouping. None of Cook’s backups—Ray Davis, Frank Gore Jr., and Ty Johnson have all suited up this season—have provided much in the way of production, so it’s a group buoyed by Cook and his gaudy six yards per carry average. Cook has 70 rushes for 421 yards and three touchdowns this season; however, he’s already fumbled twice. He also has provided next to nothing as a receiver, catching just six of ten targets for 24 yards. What have Cook’s backups done? Well, the aforementioned trio has just four total carries this season—not a typo—for 12 yards. Davis has one reception for four yards, while Johnson has six receptions for 59 yards. Cook is a dynamic rusher, but I’d really like to see the Bills incorporate some sort of change-of-pace out of the backfield. Whether that means using someone else to rest his legs or using Cook as a receiver more is up to the coaching staff, but right now, Buffalo’s a little predictable in how they’re deploying Cook. Wide Receivers: B This is another grouping where there has definitely been some good—DJ Moore’s first game as a Bill, Keon Coleman’s performance against New England—but the overall production of the group leaves some room for improvement. Moore’s effectiveness has been hampered by a shoulder injury that he suffered in the second quarter of Buffalo’s second game, a 41-31 win over the Detroit Lions. After catching five passes for 100 yards and a score against the Houston Texans in the opening week, he’s caught just seven passes for 78 yards in the three games since. Buffalo really targets three receivers in the passing game, as Moore (20 targets), Khalil Shakir (a team-high 23 targets), and Coleman (16 targets) all outpace the fourth receiver, Joshua Palmer (9 targets) in that category. Shakir was invisible for much of the season until the New England game, too, as he essentially doubled his season totals by catching seven passes for 82 yards on the afternoon. Coleman has been extremely efficient, catching 14 of his 16 targets, and he has more receiving yards (217) than anyone in his positional group. Palmer has caught two highlight-reel touchdowns, but he’s also missed a handful of easy grabs, and he has shown little ability to win in a contested catch situation. Rookie Skyler Bell has yet to see the field, and Greg Dortch hasn’t seen a target in the passing game. A healthy Moore amplifies this group, and I wouldn’t be mad at a shuffle of the gameday jerseys to see if Bell can provide some juice. Aside from the two touchdowns, it wouldn’t be difficult for him to match Palmer’s production (three catches on nine targets for 80 yards). Tight Ends: B+ This likely would have been an A or an A- if the gameplan on Sunday had actually included the team’s best receiver. Sure, the Patriots knew that they had to key on Dalton Kincaid, but how does the head coach and play caller allow them to entirely eighty-six No. 86? Kincaid leads the team in receptions (15; tied with Shakir) and receiving yards (270). He didn’t see his second target of the game on Sunday until the Bills’ final drive, and that’s when he made his first catch. Dawson Knox has caught all six of his targets for 30 yards and a score. Jackson Hawes has just one target, but he remains a menace as an in-line blocker. Speaking of blocking, Kincaid has improved tremendously in that area; while he once was a liability on the outside, he’s done a nice job clearing space for Cook in the run game. It’s inexcusable for someone with Kincaid’s talent to see two targets in a game, and it’s inexplicable why that would happen in a game where DJ Moore was out with an injury. The tight end group has pulled its weight. Offensive Line: C+ This grade is a tale of two halves. In the run game, the blocking has been close to A-level. In the pass game, there are too many instances where guys who are paid handsomely are losing one-on-ones to sustain such a high mark. Dion Dawkins, for example, is having a rough go of it at left tackle. He lost weight in the offseason to improve his quickness and agility, but I’ve seen him lose battle against bull rushes far too often this season. There’s a lot of lean and reach in his technique, as well, which doesn’t help that bull rush. His Pro Football Focus grades have been good this season, but that’s because of his run block grade (85.3, third-best at tackle) boosting his pass-block grade (68.3, 35th among tackles). Spencer Brown has the opposite issue, as the eye test has shown him to be great for much of the season, but his PFF grades are middling. The interior offensive line has seen some mixed returns, as well, with Connor McGovern anchoring (he appeared to allow his first sack in a very long time against the Chargers, but it seems that it wasn’t credited to him), O’Cyrus Torrence showing improvement, and Alec Anderson playing some hit-or-miss ball. Overall, this is a unit that seems to have taken a brief step back from last season, as they’ve been strong in run blocking and not nearly as good in pass protection. Hopefully, as the group adjusts to having Anderson in the lineup full-time, they’ll continue to gel and improve as the…

title: Buffalo Bills are finding the right way to use Keon Coleman, and they must stick with it
summary: The Buffalo Bills need to be as careful with Keon Coleman as I will be writing this article. Coleman is starting to understand his on-field shortcomings and how to work around them to become an asset to the Buffalo Bills passing game. His 116-yard performance in Week 4’s loss to the Patriots was the second-highest […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills need to be as careful with Keon Coleman as I will be writing this article. Coleman is starting to understand his on-field shortcomings and how to work around them to become an asset to the Buffalo Bills passing game. His 116-yard performance in Week 4’s loss to the Patriots was the second-highest yardage total to date in his NFL career — behind a 134-yard performance I frankly don’t have much recollection of in a 34-10 throttling of the Titans at home in 2024. After Week 4, Coleman’s yards-per-route-run figure of 2.38 is nearly double what it was a season ago, and he’s hauled in two of his three contested-catch opportunities in the first month of the season. Contested-catch win rate isn’t particularly sticky from season to season or week to week. But winning more of those opportunities than he loses — even this early — is a step in the right direction for someone who’s hovered between 30-40% dating back to the 2023 campaign at Florida State. But Coleman is still not separating at a regular clip. Has he shown slightly better releases against press off the line of scrimmage? Yes. Is he ever going to be a consistent man-coverage winner in the NFL? Most likely not. Now, success at receiver in today’s NFL isn’t strictly dictated by separation ability against man coverage. There’s more that goes into playing the position well, but either the natural athletic talent to spring yourself free from coverage or the refined skilled to allow you to do so remains king. What I’ve noticed with Coleman early in Year 3 is that he’s finally understanding how to get open and “stay open” against zone. He’s not running through voids in coverage. He’s processing said coverage faster, and it’s clicking faster in his mind that he might actually already be open in some stages of the route. Also, he’s seemingly getting that some creativity in the route is often needed to either get open or stay open for Josh Allen. The NFL moves at a ridiculously fast pace. Two weeks ago, Joe Brady was the toast of the town in Buffalo for his offensive ingenuity. Now many Bills fans think his offense is stagnant and predictable. I even wrote a critique-based column on the Bills needing to get back to their tight-end heavy ways of Weeks 1 and 2. For the record, I don’t think Brady is suddenly calling a dull and easy-to-defend offense. But one indisputably smart wrinkle from Brady pertains to Coleman entering Week 5. Brady is deploying Coleman more in the slot and in-line (essentially attached to the line of scrimmage) than ever before. Through four games, Coleman has run 16.5% of his routes from the slot and 6.8% of his routes in-line. Combined that’s 23.3% As a rookie, Coleman appeared in the slot + in-line on 10.8% of his routes. Last year, that figure was 18.7% in the regular season and sunk to 2.4% in the playoffs. And even when Coleman has been the “outside” receiver in this offense, Brady has increased the tight-split look before the snap, essentially giving Coleman slot-esque positioning. As a rookie and in 2025, Coleman ran routes on the outside from those reduced splits — closer to the offensive tackle — around 35% of the time in both seasons. Through four games, those instances are up to 50.9%, per Fantasy Points Data. In short, Brady is providing Coleman more room to operate based on pre-snap alignment alone. That’s precisely what he needs to be maximized as a large-body, athletic-but-not-twitchy weapon at the intermediate level and down the field. And here’s where the Bills have to be careful. They have to stick with the curated deployment of Coleman. Just because he’s fresh off a 100-yard performance does not mean he’s now ready to move into a classic X or Z role, staying mostly stagnant near the sideline. He’s not suddenly ready to win against more man coverage and safeties more regularly over the top. He can’t become a target-magnet either. And as long as DJ Moore is healthy, I really don’t believe he will be. The Bills tried this type of experiment with former stud WR4 Gabe Davis. They moved him to an elevated pass-game role, and it didn’t work. He couldn’t get open nearly as much as he needed to. Coleman is still young — only 23 — but the Bills should have a reasonably good sense of who he is as a receiver and who he isn’t. He’s undoubtedly growing as a player, his skills are sharpening, and Brady appears to understand an optimal way to use him on the field. To continue Coleman’s growth, regardless of who’s healthy, who’s not, or who the Bills are playing, they need to continue to stay on this new track for his specific utilization.
author: Chris Trapasso

title: Bills snap counts: Four tight ends is suddenly one too many
summary: Buffalo’s first loss of the season came with plenty of questions. The snap counts provide a few clues, but they certainly don’t make the Bills’ 29-26 loss to the New England Patriots any easier to digest. The Bills logged 59 offensive snaps, 76 defensive snaps and 26 special teams snaps. That is a lot of […]
full_text: Buffalo’s first loss of the season came with plenty of questions. The snap counts provide a few clues, but they certainly don’t make the Bills’ 29-26 loss to the New England Patriots any easier to digest. The Bills logged 59 offensive snaps, 76 defensive snaps and 26 special teams snaps. That is a lot of time for a struggling defense to spend on the field, especially when the coverage kept giving Drake Maye somewhere to go with the football. And on offense? There is a glaring reality that the Bills do not need four tight ends. Even if all four made an appearance. Every snap for the offensive line, with some uncomfortable questions Josh Allen and all five starting offensive linemen played all 59 offensive snaps. Alec Anderson, Dion Dawkins, O’Cyrus Torrence, Spencer Brown and Connor McGovern handled the entire workload. Unfortunately, being available for every snap and playing well on every snap are two different things. Dawkins’ pass protection is becoming a concern for me. The hope was that his weight loss would help him get off the snap quicker, but what I’m seeing lately is a left tackle getting overpowered all too often. Buffalo needs to find a way to give Allen more dependable protection, whether that means help with an additional tight end (since we have so many) or better execution from the players already out there. Something needs to change. Four tight ends, but what did Buffalo get out of it? Dawson Knox led the tight ends with 36 snaps (61%), followed closely by Dalton Kincaid with 35 (59%). Jackson Hawes played 14 (24%), while Keleki Latu appeared for one offensive snap (2%). I’m still struggling to see the payoff. If Buffalo needs additional help in pass protection, that group ought to be part of the solution. There is some context worth keeping, though: Latu played 18 special-teams snaps (69%). His offensive role was tiny, but his role elsewhere was substantial. Is it enough to keep 4 tight ends on the active roster? James Cook: Still waiting for the football Cook played 35 offensive snaps (just 59%). Ty Johnson handled 19 (32%), and Ray Davis played four (7%). Cook’s 12 carries produced 75 yards and a touchdown, good for 6.3 yards per attempt. Another productive afternoon. Another afternoon where I’m asking why he didn’t get more opportunities. Being on the field for more than half the offensive snaps is fine. Actually giving him the ball when he’s running that effectively would be even better. Coleman leads the receivers Keon Coleman led Buffalo’s receivers with 46 snaps (78%), just ahead of Khalil Shakir’s 45 (76%). Joshua Palmer played 35 (59%), DJ Moore played 23 (39%), and Greg Dortch played two (3%). Moore re-aggravated his shoulder injury sidelining him yet again. Coleman made his workload count with six catches for 116 yards and the fourth-quarter touchdown that briefly put Buffalo ahead. On a frustrating afternoon, his emergence was one of the few things worth feeling good about. Dortch’s bigger role came on special teams, where he played 11 snaps (42%). Hawes added 10 (38%), Davis five (19%), and Johnson four (15%). Lloyd Cushenberry and Austin Corbett each played four special-teams snaps without appearing on offense. A heavy workload at linebacker, with disappointing impact Terrel Bernard played 70 defensive snaps (92%). He wasn’t quite out there for every play, but he was close, and that much playing time makes his lack of impact even harder to overlook. There are stretches where it feels like he’s missing from the action. Buffalo needs its inside linebacker to do more than occupy a spot on the snap-count sheet. Dorian Williams played 52 snaps (68%). I commended him last week. This week, I thought he looked even worse than Bernard, particularly in pass coverage. That is a pretty uncomfortable reversal in seven days. The Bills have problems in the middle of the defense and in the secondary. When both areas struggle at the same time, the pass rush can only cover up so much. Plenty of work for a secondary that couldn’t close the door Davison Igbinosun, Cole Bishop and C.J. Gardner-Johnson played all 76 defensive snaps. Maxwell Hairston, who was exploited all afternoon, was nearly a full-time participant with 74 (97%). Damar Hamlin and Dee Alford each played 24 (32%). Christian Benford did not suit up because of an injury, leaving Buffalo without one of its starting cornerbacks. That absence is important context for Igbinosun’s full workload and Hairston’s nearly full afternoon. The Bills were already shorthanded, and the coverage problems made that absence feel even bigger. It would have been nice to see Kani Walker take a snap or two on defense with the struggles of the secondary but the decision was made to keep his snaps solely on special teams. Watching Maye find answers behind Buffalo’s pressure was maddening. The Bills could disrupt the pocket, but too often the coverage failed to finish the job. The snap counts show who was out there. They don’t make what happened behind the pass rush any prettier. The edge tandem keeps working Bradley Chubb played 63 snaps (83%), with Greg Rousseau right behind him at 62 (82%). Both were among the brighter spots in my view, creating disruption and contributing against the run. Deone Walker led the interior defensive line with 59 snaps (78%). DeWayne Carter played 45 (59%), Greg Gaines 31 (41%), Landon Jackson 29 (38%), and Ed Oliver 24 (32%). Oliver’s reduced workload was injury-related, with everyone else’s increased playing time coming because of Oliver’s injury. Elsewhere in the rotation, Parker played 20 defensive snaps (26%), Kaleb Elarms-Orr played 16 (21%), and Hoecht played 15 (20%). Special-teams workload Joe Andreessen and Sam Franklin led Buffalo with 21 special-teams snaps apiece (81%), followed by Javon Solomon with 19 (73%). None of the three played a defensive snap. Hoecht added 17 (65%), Elarms-Orr 15 (58%), and Hamlin and Parker 14 each (54%). Kani Walker played 11 (42%), Tyler Bass 10 (38%), and Reid Ferguson, T. Couch and T. Doman eight apiece (31%). What’s next? Buffalo is still 3-1. But there is plenty to fix before the next snap-count sheet arrives, starting with better protection for Allen, especially if he’s making a consensus decision to not run, Moore opportunities for Cook, and a defense that needs to make its time on the field count. Unfortunately, the next test for the defense comes against a better offense, under the Monday night lights in Los Angeles. The Bills have a week to find answers, and two tough games heading into their bye week. If they are not careful they can go from 3-0 to 3-3 very easily.

title: Buffalo Bills need to revert to multiple tight end ways on offense
summary: The Buffalo Bills were the talk of the NFL after the first two weeks of the season not only because they were averaging 38.5 points per game and started 2-0. In the increasing analytics-happy or at least analytics aware NFL universe, Buffalo’s utilization of 13 personnel (three tight ends on the field at the same […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills were the talk of the NFL after the first two weeks of the season not only because they were averaging 38.5 points per game and started 2-0. In the increasing analytics-happy or at least analytics aware NFL universe, Buffalo’s utilization of 13 personnel (three tight ends on the field at the same time) was applauded by the masses as the Bills standing away from the crowd — ironically alongside the Rams, their Week 5 opponent — to maximize offensive efficiency and keep defenses guessing run or pass. The past two weeks, the heavy lean into 13 personnel has all but officially vanished. Bills 13 personnel rate by week, per @SumerSports : Wk 1: 40.4% Wk 2: 29.0% Wk 3: 28.6% Wk 4: 13.0% — Shawn Syed (@SyedSchemes) October 5, 2026 The crazy part about the relatively very low rate in Week 4… of course DJ Moore left in the first half and didn’t return. That development was begging for the Bills to go revert to their previously trademark tight end trio, and they decided against it. Also I can’t be convinced the Bills lack of 13 personnel against New England was game-script oriented. No team ever held more than a touchdown lead throughout. The key piece to this group — Dalton Kincaid, only appeared on 35 snaps in Week 4, his first game under 40 snaps this season. For the Bills sake, it should be the only time he plays fewer than 40 snaps. His presence on the field is too valuable. Sure, Kincaid isn’t going to move people in the run game like Dawson Knox or Jackson Hawes. But if you’re sitting in a multiple tight-end set around 30-40% of the time, the opposition can’t always assume it’s a pass play. They have to match with more base defense with less coverageWhen it’s a hardly-used grouping, it doesn’t have nearly as much of a disguising effect. If Moore can’t play against the Rams, the Bills need to live in multiple tight-end personnel groupings as much as reasonably possible. Doesn’t just have to be 13. Filter through the tight end combinations in 12 personnel. In fact, the Bills have dipped to 23rd in EPA per play when in 13 — the last two weeks have severely hurt those figures — but are 4th in EPA per play when using 12 personnel. And this push isn’t simply schematic. Buffalo’s tight end trio needs to regularly block more effectively for the multiple-tight end sets to work well for the ground game too. Kincaid in particular. Still have yet to chart a snap where Dalton Kincaid was in-line and the Bills ran to his side I’ve charted 12 games of his now between this year and last year. Not one. Tucker Kraft was used on 92 (!) in the same 8 game sample last year: https://t.co/rHs2WHqbaj pic.twitter.com/WKqJWiuaeU — Max Toscano (@maxtoscano1) October 6, 2026 Without Moore, the Bills should be shying away from 11 personnel (three receivers on the field). Without Moore, the receiver group is not a strength of the team. The tight end group, running back, and offensive line are the strengths beyond Josh Allen. Like Bruce wrote earlier today, the Bills need to look backwards to find answers to their problems. Here’s to more multiple tight-end sets from the Bills on Monday Night Football against the Rams and in the foreseeable future.

title: Panthers vs. Lions game review: M-V-P, M-V-P
summary: When you get your first opportunity to host a Sunday Night Football game in over a decade, you want to make the most of it. If the chants ringing out through the stadium at various points of the broadcast were any indication, I’d say that mission was accomplished. Bryce Young may not have heard it, […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - OCTOBER 4: Bryce Young #9 of the Carolina Panthers reacts as he takes the field against the Detroit Lions prior to an NFL football game at Bank of America Stadium on October 4, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images When you get your first opportunity to host a Sunday Night Football game in over a decade, you want to make the most of it. If the chants ringing out through the stadium at various points of the broadcast were any indication, I’d say that mission was accomplished. Bryce Young may not have heard it, or was too humble to acknowledge it, but the millions of people watching the only game on TV did. For this week’s game review, let’s take a look at his performance and how it’s worthy of the chants. While Young has had games with 300+ passing yards, it’s the considerable jump in consistency that’s new and is adding some weight behind the MVP buzz. Not only that, but the ‘lows’ aren’t as low and he still puts up well over 200 yards instead of well under. The raw passing production also comes with several notable more advanced metrics that add more context to just how well Young performed. On 41 attempts, Young completed 8.5% more passes than expected, including the 3rd and 14 strike to Teteiroa McMillan that’s the 18th most improbable completion of the season so far, according to Next Gen Stats. Young still manages to generate an EPA of 0.47 even while pressured at a rate that’s (depending on which site you look on) more than any other quarterback in the NFL. Now, I do believe that there is some inflation to that statistic. While there is definitely no doubt that the offensive line has left much to be desired while being down several starters and losing Monroe Freeling during the game, some of those pressures are caused by the Panthers leaving defenders intentionally unblocked as the read defender in the Panthers run-pass-option concepts. A huge uptick in those plays caught the Detroit Lions off guard, and isolated their defenders in space and put them in conflict; do they take the bait and crash down on Young? On several occasions an unblocked player was credited with a pressure while Young threw the ball to an open receiver running through a passing lane that the defender just vacated. JT does an outstanding job diagramming the Panthers RPO that crushed the Lions multiple times @theqbschool (I'm going to assume Darrell Bevell brought this with him from the Dolphins) https://t.co/ecwVuuh5Sc pic.twitter.com/fpBxhl6UWL — Josh Norris (@JoshNorris) October 7, 2026 But it’s Young’s development and ability as a passer that allows the offense to operate this way. Few quarterbacks in the NFL can handle that much onus being put onto them; to handle an unblocked defender speeding at them and choosing between 3 different routes that his stature likely doesn’t even allow him to fully see. It’s not just adequate, in many aspects it’s elite. According to TruMedia, Young has a 72% precision pass rate in the middle of the field, the highest mark in the league. When you make an argument for Young as an MVP, or say his Week 4 performance is the quality you’d expect from an MVP candidate, it’s those aspects that should be considered. When things aren’t going as expected (see: injuries to Jalen Coker, Xavier Legette, Ikem Ekwonu, Taylor Moton, Damien Lewis, Monroe Freeling, Brady Christensen, Jonathon Brooks, Trevor Etienne and Chris Brazzell) what can he do to make it work? In other words…. how does Young still provide value? Right now, Young is putting himself in the line of fire and producing at a level that rivals the best quarterbacks in the NFL. Can it continue like this? If it does, don’t be surprised if those chants are heard throughout Charlotte in December.

title: Chicago Bears Stock Watch: Monangai rising as Swift falls
summary: Sunday morning, I found myself getting nervous. As the Chicago Bears game approached, I found myself doubting the optimism and enthusiasm I saw online from fellow Bears fans. I’ve seen the Bears start backup quarterbacks so many times, I thought. And Tyson Bagent is far less experienced than Case Keenum. Surely, there was a chance […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - OCTOBER 04: Kyle Monangai #25 of the Chicago Bears reacts after rushing for yards during the fourth quarter of the game against the New York Jets at Soldier Field on October 04, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Jessie Alcheh/Getty Images) | Getty Images Sunday morning, I found myself getting nervous. As the Chicago Bears game approached, I found myself doubting the optimism and enthusiasm I saw online from fellow Bears fans. I’ve seen the Bears start backup quarterbacks so many times, I thought. And Tyson Bagent is far less experienced than Case Keenum. Surely, there was a chance he would play badly enough for the Jets to hang around and possibly win. Then the game started. I have long been a “hope for the best, expect the worst” fan. Beaten down by years of high offseason expectations, only to be disappointed by the on-field result. It’s time I adjust my expectations. This is the Ben Johnson era. He is one of the best at scheming and game planning. He almost always has his team ready to play. The Bears have one of the best coaches in the league. And that means they’re going to be in way more games than they’re out of. Get used to it. Stock up Kyle Monangai, RB – 4.9 yards per rush, 146 rushing yards and two touchdowns. The seventh-round pick has endeared himself to many Bears fans. He is a driving force of Chicago’s rushing attack. Rome Odunze, WR – After a week of chatter about how disappointing he’s been, Rome came out with his best game of the young season. He caught six of seven targets for 94 yards. And they were at all levels — a long of 37 yards and even just short routes and quick screens. Hopefully, he builds on this. Colston Loveland, TE – Finally, the guy fans have been longing to see all summer got involved in the passing game. His blocking highlights were still there, as he helped pave the way for Chicago’s 232 yards on the ground. But he also caught six of his nine targets for 57 yards. Stock down D’Andre Swift, RB – We’ll see how long Swift remains in Johnson’s doghouse following his second lost fumble of the season. Swift didn’t return to the game after he lost a fumble in the third quarter. However, he’s too important to stay on the bench. I imagine the message was sent, but now it’s up to Swift to bounce back. Tyson Bagent, QB – He won; he was efficient (completed 73.5 percent of his passes), but it’s never good when your team wins by 11 and some amount of fans and pundits think you should be benched. Bagent doesn’t have the arm strength for some of the over-the-middle throws. But the coaches believe in him, and he’s going to get another start this weekend. I just don’t know if I feel as comfortable with that as I was maybe two months ago. Tory Taylor, P – He got no action this week. Poor guy. He must’ve been super bored. Who was up and down in your opinion? Let us know in the comments.

title: Bears-Jets Upon Further Review: A Closer Look at the Referees
summary: Hello Chicago Bears fans! This one is a fun one, as the Chicago Bears dominated the New York Jets and the laundry was one-sided in our favor. Tyson Bagent started for Caleb Williams and threw four interceptions – only one of which counted as a result of Jets penalties. Kyle Monangai ran for 146 and […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - OCTOBER 04: Jowon Briggs #91 and Will McDonald IV #9 of the New York Jets tackle D'Andre Swift #4 of the Chicago Bears during the first quarter of the game at Soldier Field on October 04, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images Hello Chicago Bears fans! This one is a fun one, as the Chicago Bears dominated the New York Jets and the laundry was one-sided in our favor. Tyson Bagent started for Caleb Williams and threw four interceptions – only one of which counted as a result of Jets penalties. Kyle Monangai ran for 146 and two scores, in the wake of two controversial goal-line reversals by the eye-in-the-sky that turned away two Swift touchdowns and gave the ball back to the Jets. Chicago held the ball for 42:45 on their way to a 3–1 record and a date with the Pack. New York had 157 yards, seven first downs, and one touchdown. Carl Cheffers’ crew accepted 16 flags: Chicago 4–29 , Jets 12–76 . However, that flag disparity hides some unseen calls if we only look at the yellow cloth on the field. The flags killed three Jets interceptions (two of which would not have been interceptions but for the flags), and “upon further review” two Bears touchdowns were deleted from the scoreboard. Same scale for judging flags: Correct, Arguable, Incorrect, Horrible. Impact weight is scaled 1–4: housekeeping, drive disruption, scoring or automatic first, wiped score or takeaway. First Quarter NYJ 0, CHI 0 Elijah Hicks (CHI), illegal block above the waist, 6 yards — 15:00. Opening kick. Zach Thomas returns to the 15; enforced back to the 6. Correct. Wt 1. Darrell Jackson Jr. (NYJ), face mask, 15 yards — 10:39. 2nd-and-8 at the NYJ 31. Monangai for 1. Jackson grabs the facemask. Ball to the NYJ 15. Chicago reaches the 1 and has a Swift touchdown reversed. Correct. Wt 3. Replay — Swift, runner broke the plane, reversed — 9:31. 2nd-and-3 at the NYJ 4. Swift right guard is ruled a touchdown on the field. Booth looks at it and brings it back: Swift to the NYJ 1 for 2 yards. This one is a pile at the goal line. You can sell the short of the plane. You can also sell that the ball got there. Clear and obvious is not met either way. Arguable. Wt 3. It is a taken-off score, but the down is not dead yet. Replay — Swift, runner broke the plane, reversed — 9:14. 4th-and-1 at the NYJ 1. Swift left guard is ruled a touchdown on the field. The replay official stops it. Reversed: no gain, short of the goal line. Turnover on downs. This is the one that fails the standard. The call on the field was a score. To take a touchdown off the board you need a frame that makes the ruling indisputable, not a better guess from upstairs. The available look is a body at the goal line with the ball at the hip. That is not clear and obvious. Incorrect. Wt 4. A touchdown that would have made it 7–0 becomes Jets ball at their own 1. New York (team), delay of game, 0 yards — 9:12. Goal-line stand just held. Enforced at the NYJ 1 before the first snap of the ensuing series. Process. Correct. Wt 1. Qwan’tez Stiggers (NYJ), illegal touch kick, 5 yards — 7:47. Wipes Austin McNamara’s 62-yard punt. Re-kick. Correct. Wt 2. Cole Kmet (CHI), false start, 5 yards — 6:42. 2nd-and-3 at midfield. Dead-ball. Correct. Wt 1. Theo Benedet (CHI), offensive holding, 10 yards — 4:58. 2nd-and-6 at the NYJ 29. Monangai’s 15-yard run comes back. Enforced at the 25: 2nd-and-12 at the NYJ 35. Arguable. Wt 2. Azareye’h Thomas (NYJ), illegal use of hands, 5 yards — 4:34. The snap of the game. 2nd-and-12. Bagent throws for Loveland. T’Vondre Sweat intercepts at the NYJ 36. Flag on Thomas. No play. Automatic first at the NYJ 30. Eight plays later Monangai scores from the 1. 0–7. Correct if the hands are on the receiver before the ball — and the crew treated it as a live foul that kills the pick. Wt 4. This is the flag that turned a Jets takeaway into the first points of the afternoon. NYJ 0, CHI 7 at 0:23. Second Quarter NYJ 0, CHI 7 New York (team), delay of game, 5 yards — 14:07. 3rd-and-10 at the NYJ 32 becomes 3rd-and-15. Geno Smith sacked by Austin Booker. Punt. Correct. Wt 2. Harrison Phillips (NYJ), defensive holding, 5 yards — 5:59. Automatic first. Arguable. Wt 2. Minkah Fitzpatrick’s interception of Bagent stands. Jets’ first pick in 21 games. They start at the CHI 34 and get a Sanders 36-yarder. 3–7. D’Angelo Ponds (NYJ), illegal contact, 5 yards — 0:43. 3rd-and-6. Second wiped interception on the Jets’ own postgame account. Automatic first. Arguable until All-22 says the contact is early and obvious. Wt 3. Santos from 30 as the half expires. 3–13. Third Quarter NYJ 3, CHI 13 New York (team), delay of game — declined — 10:12. 4th-and-12. New York (team), delay of game, 5 yards — 7:05. 4th-and-4. They still kick Sanders from 30. 6–13. Correct. Wt 1. Brandon Stephens (NYJ), face mask, 15 yards — 6:23. 2nd-and-4. Fifteen yards and a first. Correct if the hand is in the cage. Wt 3. Monangai’s 5-yard score at 2:26 makes it 6–20. Fourth Quarter NYJ 6, CHI 20 Santos from 21 at 10:01. 6–23. Sam Roush (CHI), offensive holding, 8 yards — 9:16. Kickoff after Isaiah Williams’ 58-yard touchdown. Sanders misses the extra point. 12–23. Return-team hold. Arguable. Wt 1. Ja’Tavion Walker (CHI), illegal block above the waist — declined — 9:16. Same kick. Demario Davis (NYJ), defensive offside, 5 yards — 8:21. 3rd-and-4. The flag Aaron Glenn tied to Brandon Stephens’ wiped interception, Chicago already up 23–12. Correct. Wt 3. D’Angelo Ponds (NYJ), defensive holding, 5 yards — 6:08. 3rd-and-8 on the 18-play clock-killer. Automatic first. Arguable. Wt 3. T’Vondre Sweat (NYJ), neutral zone infraction, 6 yards — 3:22. 4th-and-1. Chicago was going to run it out. Sweat jumps. First down. Drive ends the game. Correct. Wt 2. Calls Against Chicago Play Grade Wt Hicks IBAW Correct 1 Swift TD reversed (2nd-and-3) Arguable 3 Swift TD reversed (4th-and-1) Incorrect 4 Kmet false start Correct 1 Benedet holding Arguable 2 Roush holding (kick) Arguable 1 Calls Against New York Play Grade Wt Jackson Jr. face mask Correct 3 Delay (goal line) Correct 1 Stiggers illegal touch Correct 2 Thomas illegal use of hands (wiped Sweat INT) Correct 4 Delay (Q2) Correct 2 Phillips defensive holding Arguable 2 Ponds illegal contact (wiped pick) Arguable 3 Delay (Q3) Correct 1 Stephens face mask Correct 3 Davis offside (wiped Stephens INT) Correct 3 Ponds defensive holding Arguable 3 Sweat NZI Correct 2 12 accepted. 8 Correct, 4 Arguable, 0 Incorrect, 0 Horrible. Three of those flags are attached to interceptions that did not count. Fitzpatrick’s pick is the one that survived, and it produced three points. Crew card: accepted flags 10 Correct, 6 Arguable. Replay adds 1 Arguable and 1 Incorrect, both on Chicago scores. Combined: 10 Correct, 7 Arguable, 1 Incorrect, 0 Horrible. Differential. Wrong-call net is one play, and it runs at Chicago: the 4th-and-1 reversal, Weight 4. New York’s damage is self-inflicted — Thomas, Davis, Ponds, Sweat. The booth’s damage is a touchdown that stood on the field and did not survive a look that was not clear. Monangai got the seven back on the next drive. The standard still failed on the snap before that. Flag of the game: the second Swift reversal, 4th-and-1, 9:14 of the first quarter. Call on the field was a touchdown. The rule for taking it off is clear and obvious. The tape is a goal-line pile. That is Incorrect, Weight 4 — a wiped score and a turnover, even in a game Chicago won anyway. Ground caused it. That is not a fumble. It is an incomplete process: down by contact,…

title: Chicago Bears Midweek Musings: Dennis Allen, Magician
summary: Some random thoughts about the Chicago Bears and other things, mostly football-related as we count down the hours until we get to watch this team play football again: I had to chuckle just a bit at the Dennis Allen love this week – not that he doesn’t deserve it, just how some Bears fans and […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 28: Offensive coordinator Press Taylor and defensive coordinator Dennis Allen of the Chicago Bears look on prior to the game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Soldier Field on September 28, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images Some random thoughts about the Chicago Bears and other things, mostly football-related as we count down the hours until we get to watch this team play football again: I had to chuckle just a bit at the Dennis Allen love this week – not that he doesn’t deserve it, just how some Bears fans and analysts are presenting it. Many came into the year saying the Bears had a bottom three defense and they were wasting the season by not doing enough on that side of the ball. Because the defense has looked sharp the last three weeks, and it can’t be a misevaluation of the talent, it’s clearly that Dennis Allen is a magician. Many of those same fans and analysts were openly questioning whether or not Allen would last in Chicago at times last year. So it goes. For my part, I was a big fan of Dennis Allen hire, and I’m a sucker for a “second year in the system” bump. I’ve also talked about the potential for the Bears defense to continue their thieving ways in 2026 with more positive game scripts. So far, so good. I get that the lack of investment made many nervous, but it’s always a good idea to let actual football be played before making a final determination. Still a long way to go, but early returns are positive. I do like the magician talk because Allen is truly good at what he does. Someone good at Photoshop, get me Dennis Allen in a magician outfit, stat. Cue Final Countdown, please. At my local gym, 95+% of people are wearing earbuds or headphones, but there’s usually loud music playing. Then the new trainer brings out a boom box turned up to 11 for his small group sessions. Plus, the one guy talking on his phone trying to shout over all the background noise. I think I need to invest in another pair of noise-canceling headphones. I’m going to hold out hope that Jaylon Johnson rounds into form and recaptures some of his old magic before hitting the panic button, but the clock is running out on Tyrique Stevenson. When Kyler Gordon returns and ramps up to a full-time role (I know, I know), Malik Muhammad is going to take over the boundary corner snaps and Tyrique will be relegated to a part-time role. All the talent in the world but can’t put it together. That dropped pick, which looked like it had a chance to be a pick-six if he drove on the ball, seemed emblematic of his season. I saw Band of Brothers released a 25th anniversary documentary. The only question is do I watch the documentary before or after my 12th rewatch of the series? We’re probably not giving enough love to Jonah Jackson. Every time we say something good about him it’s usually after talking about Darnell Wright or Joe Thuney. He deserves his own vase of flowers because he’s killing it. Kudos to Ben Johnson for knowing how to best use Jackson where his previous play caller couldn’t figure it out… My best friend drove two hours to watch the game with me last weekend. We set up a TV in the garage, grilled out on a beautiful October day, and watched our favorite team dogwalk the poor Jets. The highlight might have been his plea for some Roschon Johnson, which was immediately answered with an explosive run. Loudest cheer of the day… I thought Tyson Bagent played an excellent game. He threw an interception, yes, and he got bailed out on another by penalty, but overall he played on time and threw catchable passes. (Yes, I know there were four total, but one was clearly a free play and the other was aided by the hold that was called as Bagent was throwing it. The screen pass into the mountain defensive tackle is the one he was bailed out on.) With the offensive infrastructure, he’s good enough to beat bad teams and keep the Bears competitive against mediocre ones. I’m not sure he can beat good teams. We’ll find out where the Packers sit in that spectrum on Sunday. I’m starting to hear rumors about Khalil Mack drawing trade interest from teams and you’d have to believe the Bears would be interested in adding him back. For Mack’s sake, you wonder if he’d be most interested in continuing his Hall of Fame career by circling back to Chicago and helping in a playoff run. He could use some post season success on his resume and might just be the perfect way to gild his fabulous career. Plus, it would give me an excuse to break out the Mack throwback jersey I bought years ago… Is Kyle Monangai the most fun Bears running back to watch since Walter Payton? I’m not saying best, I’m saying the most fun. Tarik Cohen was a lot of fun but not necessarily as a running back. Forte was smooth, Thomas Jones will always hold a special place in my heart, but neither brought me the pure joy I get from watching Monangai. He’s the perfect Bears running back. You got any musings? Hit the comments and let me know what’s up.

title: Chicago Bears Week 5 power rankings roundup
summary: In three out of their first four games of the season, the Chicago Bears have dominated their opponents. The Bears now have a top-10 scoring offense and defense. They’re also top three in offensive yards and defense yards allowed. Now the Bears will hit the road and go to their biggest rival’s home stadium to […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - OCTOBER 4: Kyle Monangai #25 of the Chicago Bears celebrates with teammates after scoring a touchdown during the second quarter against the New York Jets at Soldier Field on October 4, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images In three out of their first four games of the season, the Chicago Bears have dominated their opponents. The Bears now have a top-10 scoring offense and defense. They’re also top three in offensive yards and defense yards allowed. Now the Bears will hit the road and go to their biggest rival’s home stadium to face the Green Bay Packers. It’s always a big game against Green Bay and it is made more important by the fact that Chicago has an 0-1 record in the division. With four games of the season done, let’s see how the rankers rank the Bears this week. WCG – Aaron Leming 9. Chicago Bears (3-1) Biggest area of concern: The defensive line. Although the defense is playing much better, it’s hard to imagine them holding up against the league’s elite offenses without being better in the trenches. Outside of Week 1, when their defense allowed 37 points and close to 500 yards of total offense, defensive coordinator Dennis Allen has this defense playing out of their minds. There’s some talent in this group, and more on the way coming back from injury, but the defensive line lacks that one true difference-maker. We’ll see if someone already on the roster can emerge as the player, but more likely, they’ll have to find it at the deadline in early November. The Athletic – Chad Graff and Josh Kendall 8. Chicago Bears (3-1) Last week: 9 Sunday: Beat Jets 23-12 Concern level: With Ben Johnson, they’re cruising It didn’t matter that, without Caleb Williams, the Bears started Case Keenum and Tyson Bagent the last two weeks (though, technically, Keenum was a starter too in Week 4). Johnson has the Bears rolling, and there isn’t a whole lot to be concerned about after they easily dispatched the Jets. PFT – Mike Florio Bears (No. 10; 3-1): Kyle Monangai may be emerging as the best tailback option. CBS Sports – Pete Prisco 8. Chicago Bears (9) They just keep running it down the opposing team’s throats to key their 3-1 start. Winning games with backup quarterbacks is impressive and says how good their run game is this season. Yahoo Sports – Frank Schwab 6. Chicago Bears (3-1, LW: 11) The Bears get a big bump, and it’s because of their defense. Chicago had a bad Week 1 on defense, and that seemed to be in line with its preseason expectations. The Bears were 25th in defensive DVOA last season and didn’t make major improvements in the offseason. But over the last three weeks the Bears’ defense has been excellent. From Week 2 through Week 4 they are third in EPA allowed per play. The only touchdowns they’ve given up in three weeks was an Eagles quarterback sneak that was snapped barely before time ran out in the first half, and a garbage time touchdown to the Jets in the fourth quarter when they led 23-6. It helps that Chicago has faced the Vikings with Carson Wentz, an Eagles offense that looks surprisingly inept and the Jets, but the results are impressive. If Chicago has an above-average defense, this is a Super Bowl contender. We all know the offense will be fine, especially when Caleb Williams returns. ESPN – Courtney Cronin 8. Chicago Bears (3-1) Week 4 result: Beat the Jets 23-12 Week 4 ranking: 11 Four words to describe the first four weeks: Dominating with different QBs. Caleb Williams (hamstring injury) led the Bears to a 59-point performance against the Panthers, Case Keenum beat the Eagles handedly, and Tyson Bagent enjoyed a thorough domination of the Jets. The Bears are No. 1 in total yards, first downs and time of possession, and they have the NFL’s best rushing offense (785 total yards). “It’s the cliché, next man up, certainly, but our guys, we know we have a lot of talent throughout this roster, from the front to the back end,” coach Ben Johnson said. “And so we always know we’re going to have a chance each and every week.” — Courtney Cronin NFL.com – Nick Shook 10. Chicago Bears (12) One of the most lopsided victories in recent memory finished in favor of Chicago, a team led by a coach who might be quarterback-proof. In the last two weeks, Ben Johnson has directed offenses led by second- and third-string quarterbacks, and the Bears haven’t missed a beat. Chicago’s win over the Jets was especially stunning when considering the time of possession (42:45 to 17:15) and total-plays differential (89 to 32), wide margins you simply don’t see in the modern NFL. It’s a testament to Johnson’s ability as a coach. USAToday – Nate Davis 10. Chicago Bears (9): After giving up 37 points in the opener, the defense has surrendered 28 − total − over the past three weeks. Doesn’t much matter who the QB1 is with that kind of margin for error. What do you think of Chicago’s rankings this week? Are the Bears properly ranked?

title: Hot Take Tuesday: Chicago Bears Have Best Coaching Staff in the League
summary: The Chicago Bears dominated the New York Jets like Michael Jordan playing pick-up ball against a toddler. It was impressive to watch. The numbers don’t even seem real. The Bears had more first downs than the Jets ran plays. The Jets didn’t convert one third down. The Bears dominated them on both sides of the […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 28: Head coach Ben Johnson and defensive coordinator Dennis Allen of the Chicago Bears reacts against the Philadelphia Eagles at Soldier Field on September 28, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chicago Bears dominated the New York Jets like Michael Jordan playing pick-up ball against a toddler. It was impressive to watch. The numbers don’t even seem real. The Bears had more first downs than the Jets ran plays. The Jets didn’t convert one third down. The Bears dominated them on both sides of the ball. They had the ball more than twice as long as the Jets. The Bears dominated them on both sides of the ball, far more than the score would suggest. And look, we can talk about the play of the offensive line. We can talk about Tyson Bagent’s strong performance. We can talk about Dayo Odeyingbo’s resurgence. But we really need to talk about the coaching. One day, Ben Johnson will be considered the best coach in the NFL. If we’re trying to be objective, he probably isn’t there yet. He’s closer to being the best offensive play caller in the league. That’s a title he may have by the end of the year (if he doesn’t have it already). But to be the best coach in the NFL, you need years of success. That’s not just a title you earn after 23 NFL games. But until that day comes, let’s talk about what the Bears do have, and that’s an absolutely lethal playcalling duo on both the offensive and defensive side of the ball. Ben Johnson’s playcalling has been incredible. But he’s doing it with an elite offensive line and excellent skill position players, albeit with a backup quarterback. Heading into the year, many of us thought more than half of Dennis Allen’s starting defense were backup-quality players. Dennis Allen has been a magician. He has his defense playing incredibly well. They are, by far, the best defensive team in the league on third downs. They are getting more pressure on opposing QBs than anyone thought was possible. And their rookies in the secondary are keeping that unit together. With these two coaches sitting atop this coaching staff, the argument can be made that they are the best duo in the NFL. If this continues, it won’t even be an argument. Right now, there’s only a handful of combinations you can even put in the Johnson/Allen class. There’s obviously Andy Reid and Steve Spagnuolo with the Chiefs. You have to consider Kevin O’Connell and Brian Flores in Minnesota. Sean McVay and Chris Shula have to be considered a pretty damn good combo with the Rams. Liam Coen and Anthony Campanile are doing great things in Jacksonville. The only other combo, I think, that you can even possibly consider is Kyle Shanahan and Raheem Morris in San Francisco. That’s six pairings that are probably atop the list. I think the way the Vikings offense looks right now, you have to put that duo outside of the top 5, even with Brian Flores doing incredible things with that defense. There’s a lot more to offense and defense than yards, but there are only two teams in the league that are in the top 5 for yards gained and yards allowed. That’s the LA Rams and the Chicago Bears. The only team that can claim that in points is the San Francisco 49ers. The Bears sit at 8th, but they’ve played the last 9 quarters with a backup QB. Sean McVay hasn’t lost Matthew Stafford. Raheem Morris has a lot more talent to work with than Dennis Allen. What the Bears duo is doing is incredible. It is quite simply the best in the league. The Bears haven’t even hit their stride yet. Caleb Williams will return. Kyler Gordon should be returning soon. Ozzy Trapilo’s return is imminent. The Bears are getting healthier. If they infuse a little more defensive talent into the roster at the trade deadline, this team can be as good as any team in the league. I will be the first to admit I didn’t see the defense playing at this level, but I still don’t think I’ve assessed the talent on the defense incorrectly. I think what Dennis Allen is doing is that impressive. We are entering a golden age of Chicago Bears football. Yes, Caleb Williams is a big part of that, but the biggest reason is the coaching. The Bears have the best staff in the league, and when that’s the case, the sky’s the limit.

title: Which quarterback gives the Bears the best chance against the Packers?
summary: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year, we ask questions of the most plugged-in Bears fans and fans across the country. With Caleb Williams still likely sidelined with a hamstring injury, Chicago Bears head coach Ben Johnson has already made his decision; he’s going with Tyson Bagent […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 28: Tyson Bagent #17 and Case Keenum #11 of the Chicago Bears stand on the sidelines during the national anthem prior to an NFL football game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Soldier Field on September 28, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year, we ask questions of the most plugged-in Bears fans and fans across the country. With Caleb Williams still likely sidelined with a hamstring injury, Chicago Bears head coach Ben Johnson has already made his decision; he’s going with Tyson Bagent at quarterback. But would the grizzled veteran Case Keenum be a better option for the Bears? Bagent now has five starts in his career, two of which were on the road, and neither of which the Bears won. Granted, those games were in 2023 when he was a rookie, and the Bears were floundering under Matt Eberflus, but playing on the road is a different animal for an NFL quarterback. Keenum has started 70 games in his career (40 on the road), including two playoff games, one of which he won. He’s also 2-0 against the Packers, including a win in Lambeau. Granted, that was 9 years ago, but experience travels, and he showed he still has some life left in his arm a couple of weeks ago on Monday Night Football. On The Score’s Bears-Jets postgame show , former Bears Olin Kreutz and Patrick Mannelly both think there should have been an internal conversation at Halas Hall, considering there’s now full tape on each backup quarterback. The game plan was different for each, but both quarterbacks tried to play within the system while making a few ill-advised throws. I honestly don’t think it matters, as both players have a good grasp of the offense and one of the best play callers in the game today in their ear. Vote in our poll questions this week! A 17th player is permitted as long as he qualifies for the NFL’s International Pathway Program. Players with no accrued seasons (rookies) and those with fewer than nine regular-season games in their lone accrued season. A maximum of ten players are allowed who have earned no more than two accrued seasons. Up to six players with unlimited accrued seasons are permitted on the practice squad. However, the number of players in the last two categories cannot exceed 10 total players. Teams can elevate up to two practice squad players for each game, but they can still only have 48 players active on game day. After the game, the elevated player(s) will revert to the practice squad. A player can be elevated up to three times, but if he’s needed after that, the team would be required to sign him to the 53-man active roster. Players on practice squads are free agents who can be signed to another team’s active roster. A player’s current club can’t block him from leaving; they can only make a counteroffer to keep him. Ultimately, it’s the player’s decision. If a player is signed away, his new team must keep him on its 53-man roster for three weeks, but if he’s released, he’ll revert to his previous team. Players signed to another active roster are also guaranteed three weeks’ salary. A practice squad player can’t sign with his team’s upcoming opponent unless he does so six days before the upcoming game or ten days prior if his team is on its bye week.
