title: Cowboys one big takeaway: CeeDee Lamb is the man
summary: CeeDee Lamb is an absolutely exceptional football player. Sunday he put on a clinic and showed the entire league he should be mentioned in every conversation about who is the top receiver in the league. Lamb’s performance against the Texans was also one for the record books. He caught 17 passes, for 189 yards and […]
full_text: Photo by David Buono/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images CeeDee Lamb is an absolutely exceptional football player. Sunday he put on a clinic and showed the entire league he should be mentioned in every conversation about who is the top receiver in the league. Lamb’s performance against the Texans was also one for the record books. He caught 17 passes, for 189 yards and scored the game-winning touchdown with 40 seconds remaining as the Cowboys erased a 10-point halftime deficit and defeated the Texans 34-30 on Sunday. It was a career-high in receptions, the third-highest yardage total of his career and, perhaps most importantly, the kind of performance Dallas needed from its best offensive player when the game was on the line. The Cowboys knew where to go Lamb entered the game already having established himself as the centerpiece of Dallas’ passing attack, but what happened against Houston took that reliance to another level. He finished the first half with six catches for 49 yards, respectable numbers that hardly suggested what was coming after halftime. Then the Cowboys began leaning on him even more heavily, and Lamb responded with 11 catches for 140 yards in the second half, including the touchdown that ultimately decided the game. That is the part that stands out. Houston knew Lamb was going to be involved. The Texans knew Prescott was going to look his way. And yet Dallas kept finding ways to get the ball into the hands of its best receiver. That is what a true No. 1 receiver is supposed to do. It is one thing to put up big numbers when a defense loses track of you or when the quarterback happens to find you on a few explosive plays. It is something completely different to become the focal point of an offense in the second half of a game, have the defense adjust accordingly and still find a way to produce. Lamb did exactly that on Sunday. Then came the catch in the clutch The numbers would have been impressive even if Dallas had lost. They would have been a footnote, though. Instead, Lamb made the play that will be remembered from this game. With Dallas trailing 30-27 and the Cowboys needing to go 74 yards to take the lead, Prescott guided the offense down the field before finding Lamb for a 12-yard touchdown with 40 seconds remaining. The catch gave Dallas a 34-30 lead and completed a comeback in which the Cowboys scored 28 second-half points. That is the difference between having a big statistical afternoon and having a performance that changes the outcome of a football game. Lamb’s 17th reception was not simply another addition to the stat sheet. It was the play that gave Dallas the lead with less than a minute remaining and put the Cowboys in position to finish off a comeback they desperately needed. After the heartbreak in Brazil the week before, Dallas needed somebody to step forward when the game became uncomfortable. Lamb did and has all season so far. One for the record books The numbers also put Lamb in some pretty rare company. His 17 receptions are now the second-most by a Cowboys player in a single game, trailing only Jason Witten, who caught 18 passes against the New York Giants in 2012. Witten was one of the most dependable players in Cowboys history, and his 18-catch performance came during a career in which he became the franchise’s all-time leader in receptions. Lamb was one catch away from matching that single-game mark more than a decade later. He also joined rare NFL company with the performance. Lamb became only the fourth player in NFL history to record at least 17 receptions, 185 receiving yards and a touchdown in the same game, joining Hall of Famers Tom Fears and Terrell Owens along with Brandon Marshall. That is a pretty good group to find yourself alongside. This is what Dallas needs from CeeDee Lamb The Cowboys are not going to win every game because Lamb catches 17 passes, and frankly, they probably shouldn’t even want him to. But when the game demands that Dallas lean on its best offensive weapon, there is no reason to apologize for doing exactly that. Lamb has now shown throughout the first four weeks that he can be productive in different ways. He has been efficient when the offense is clicking, explosive when Dallas needs chunk plays and, against Houston, almost impossible to keep away from the football when the Cowboys needed a comeback. The Cowboys have plenty of questions elsewhere on the roster. The defense remains inconsistent, at best. The pass rush has struggled to create pressure. The offensive line has had some problems and the Cowboys just spent the previous week watching a winnable game slip away in the final seconds against Baltimore. What they can count on, however, is that when Dak Prescott needs someone to make a play, CeeDee Lamb is going to be there. Sunday in Houston was the latest and perhaps clearest example. Lamb didn’t just have a career day. He gave the Cowboys exactly what a franchise receiver is supposed to give them when the game is hanging in the balance: production, reliability and, when Dallas needed it most, the play that changed the game. CeeDee Lamb is a dog, and after what he did in Houston, the Cowboys should have no problem making sure everybody else remembers it.
author: Jorge Guajardo

title: Cowboys injuries: Tyler Smith remains limited Tuesday
summary: Despite alternating wins and losses to open the season, the Dallas Cowboys opened the week as heavy favorites with a short time to prepare for the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.   The Cowboys are hoping to get some key players back this week and then get a mini-bye week before a Sunday night matchup against the […]
full_text: Photo by Ric Tapia/Getty Images | Getty Images Despite alternating wins and losses to open the season, the Dallas Cowboys opened the week as heavy favorites with a short time to prepare for the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. The Cowboys are hoping to get some key players back this week and then get a mini-bye week before a Sunday night matchup against the Green Bay Packers. That said, the injuries impacting the Buccaneers have also tipped the scales in favor of the Cowboys. After today’s practice, here is the state of both teams. Week 5 Injury Report (10/6/26) – Tampa Bay @Buccaneers vs. Dallas Cowboys: https://t.co/qL6rHh823d #WeAreTheKrewe pic.twitter.com/xI41pFFZOt — Buccaneers Communications (@BuccaneersComms) October 6, 2026 Cornerback Cobie Durant (hamstring) did not practice as expected. Durant is believed to be unavailable for at least a few weeks. Also, linebacker DeMarvion Overshown did not practice again today with the team. Initially, there was hope that Overshown would be back Thursday, but given where he is with his health, and the time off in between, the team may hold off against the Buccaneers. Pro Bowl guard Tyler Smith was not upgraded today to a full participant but optimism remains high that he’ll be coming back from the thumb injury that landed him on injured reserve to start the season. For the Buccaneers, Antoine Winfield Jr. (rib) did not practice today, and the team expects him to be out this week. Also, starting quarterback Baker Mayfield (thumb) didn’t practice once again, foreshadowing what will be his second consecutive missed start. Meanwhile, Reuben Bain (groin/shoulder) was a full participant again today and suffered no setbacks.
author: LP Cruz

title: The highs and lows of a chaotic Cowboys victory
summary: Watching the Dallas Cowboys toggle between greatness and embarrassment has been taxing on their fanbase, but after Sunday’s performance, they are showing no sign of changing things up. This past weekend’s game against the Houston Texans was another wild ride, featuring a little bit of everything, making it really hard to figure them out. After […]
full_text: Mandatory Credit: Thomas Shea-Imagn Images Watching the Dallas Cowboys toggle between greatness and embarrassment has been taxing on their fanbase, but after Sunday’s performance, they are showing no sign of changing things up. This past weekend’s game against the Houston Texans was another wild ride, featuring a little bit of everything, making it really hard to figure them out. After taking a closer look at the game film, how do we feel about this football team? They have the firepower to compete with anyone, but they have also shown an ability to self-destruct at the worst moments. What did we get this time? Let’s run down the things we learned after further review. The Cowboys have a really good offense. The first part of the game might have made us question that statement, but we must remember that the Texans have a really great defense. When you think about how the offensive line handled Will Anderson Jr., who still looked amazing, and all the talented players they had upfront, it was an impressive showing. Yes, it was a struggle early. The Texans were content rushing four defenders and forcing Dak Prescott to sift through his progressions to find open receivers. He had problems at times. Houston’s coverage was tight, forcing Prescott to hold the ball, look around, and occasionally fire into dangerously tight windows. The Cowboys are lucky that one of Prescott’s tipped balls did not fall into enemy hands. While the first half was rough, the offense eventually started figuring things out. The play-calling looked miles better as the game went on, and Prescott made some great last-second adjustments at the line. At times, they turned a smothering Texans defense into a group that got confused and got turned around on plays, leaving receivers wide open. And when that happened, Prescott capitalized. Everyone got involved. What more can you say about CeeDee Lamb? He is truly sensational. George Pickens was not targeted much, but that didn’t stop him from making a couple of big plays, including another one of his patented spectacular catches. Jake Ferguson didn’t have a good game, but he came through when it mattered with a clutch fourth-down catch. And we cannot say enough about Brevyn Spann-Ford. If you go back and watch any successful running play from this game, you will find that guy wrestling a defender into submission to help spring the runner. You have to love his self-sacrificing playing style. Defensively, it was a frustrating watch at times. It wasn’t fun to watch the Texans come out with bootlegs and misdirection plays as the Cowboys defense falls for those fakes every time. When C.J. Stroud took off for a nice first-down run on Houston’s opening possession, fans collectively muttered ‘here we go again.’ Fortunately, the quarterback run-a-thon that plagued Dallas in previous weeks did not continue on Sunday. That early scramble was basically it for Stroud on the ground. The Cowboys’ entire run defense was exceptional. Are we feeling better about Quinnen Williams? He was outstanding, constantly blowing up plays in the backfield against the run and even picking up a sack. He and the entire interior defensive line came to play. The secondary struggled, though. Even with a strong debut from new cornerback Joey Porter Jr. , the unit had glaring issues in coverage. DaRon Bland was picked on early and often, giving up several big plays. It also looked like rookie safety Caleb Downs had some trouble handling coverage shifts while playing a deeper safety role in this game. He is clearly a much better, more impactful player when he is allowed to hunt near the line of scrimmage. On the bright side, there was a massive improvement in getting off the field on third downs. That was refreshing. There were four separate instances where Houston drives lasted four plays or less. Giving the Cowboys offense more opportunities definitely helped fuel the comeback. They just have to figure out how to stop giving up chunk plays in the passing game. Nico Collins absolutely killed them in the first half, though the defense deserves credit for tightening up and keeping him relatively quiet after halftime except for a touchdown. The defensive line came away with two sacks, but that shouldn’t be all that surprising. In fact, it could be viewed as a bit of a letdown considering how bad the Texans’ offensive line is. Getting consistent pressure on the quarterback remains a major concern for this defense. You have to applaud the unit’s resiliency in the second half. After giving up a touchdown drive on a short field following a big Houston kickoff return, the defense clamped down and forced two consecutive quick stops. That gave the Cowboys offense exactly what it needed to string together three straight second-half touchdown drives and climb back into the game. Still, allowing an 87-yard drive late in the fourth quarter that took less than five minutes was tough to witness. That possession acts as a bit of a dark cloud on an otherwise solid second-half showing by the defense. It doesn’t inspire confidence, especially since we know there will be moments later this season when Dallas will have to rely on a game-saving stop. Hopefully, they will have some things worked out by then. Special teams remain a weird, confusing entity. Why is this unit struggling to keep defenders from sneaking through the line and blocking Brandon Aubrey’s long field goals? There is plenty of debate on whether the coaching staff should even attempt those deep kicks, especially since those recent misses turned into direct points for the Texans. But when you have an accurate, long-distance cheat code like Aubrey, you are playing indoors, and you desperately need points, it seems perfectly reasonable to trot him out there. The man has made more 60-yard field goals than anyone else on planet Earth. Special teams coordinator Nick Sorensen is rightfully under fire because his unit has been all over the place. One positive thing we should recognize is how the Cowboys dominated the starting field position following kicks. In this game, the Cowboys started inside their own 25-yard-line just once, compared to seven times for the Texans. Aubrey’s squib kicks were spot on in this one, with one hitting right on the 20-yard-line mark while staying perfectly within the landing zone. The coverage was excellent, minus that one time when they allowed the long return. As is tradition with this special teams group lately, you get some great stuff mixed in with some bad stuff. The win is big, as a loss would have demoralized the team. The Cowboys showed they have the mental toughness to fight through a deficit and actually finish things off. If they can build on the offensive rhythm while cleaning up the breakdowns in the secondary, this team has a chance to be a contender down the stretch. But if they can’t fix their coverage lapses and special teams blunders continue to pop up, this team can only go so far.
author: Dan Rogers

title: The Parker Report: Defense’s growth continues
summary: The Dallas Cowboys defense continued its growth this week versus the Houston Texans. There’s still a ways to go. Let’s take a look at how they performed this week. Team stats allowed Against the Texans, the Cowboys defense allowed three touchdowns and three field goals. Two of the field goals were on drives starting at […]
full_text: Photo by David Buono/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys defense continued its growth this week versus the Houston Texans. There’s still a ways to go. Let’s take a look at how they performed this week. Team stats allowed Against the Texans, the Cowboys defense allowed three touchdowns and three field goals. Two of the field goals were on drives starting at the Dallas 48 and the Dallas 45 in the first half. Dallas struggled against C.J. Stroud and Nico Collins throughout the game. The Texans quarterback threw for 347 yards and finished with a rating of 126.7. Coming back from an injury, Collins recorded 118 receiving yards on seven catches, scoring twice. The Texans run game never got going in this matchup. Dallas let up just 62 yards on 19 carries, marking their best performance of the season against opposing running backs. Individual stat leaders Malik Hooker and Caleb Downs tied for the lead in tackles, accounting for seven apiece. Each would finish with five solo. The Cowboys pass rush woke up late with Rashan Gary and Quinnen Williams sacking the quarterback once apiece. Malik Hooker led the team with two pass breakups in his first game back from injury. Advanced analytics The EPA allowed per play split ranks the Cowboys 10th in run defense in week four, but an abysmal 29th in pass defense (SumerSports). The poor EPA allowed in the pass game is directly tied to explosive plays. The Texans carried a 16% explosive play rate – eight explosives on 50 qualifying snaps. Nico Collins, Jaylin Noel, Xavier Hutchinson, Kayshon Boutte, Cade Stover, and Dalton Schultz all had plays of 20 yards or greater. The hope for Dallas is that newly acquired Joey Porter Jr. will help shut down the secondary’s leakage. How’d the rookies look? Caleb Downs finished the game tied for the team lead in tackles. He wasn’t a hugely impactful player on the day though. Depending on the called coverage, it looks like he gave up his first receiving touchdown of the year. Still, he made big time solo tackles in open space and continues to provide the defense with juice. Jaishawn Barham didn’t pop off on the stats sheet this week. He would finish the game with just one solo tackle. To his credit, not much was getting past the defensive front in the run game. He did flash a handful of times on blitzes, forcing the running back into the waiting arms of other defenders. Malachi Lawrence has been disappointing disappointing. Maybe hopes were set too high, but it felt like the rookie might have a chance for his first sack against the porous Texans offensive line. He finished with just one solo tackle and zero sacks on the day. He is still carrying an incredible pass rush win rate. He’s just having a tough time converting that into sacks, as is typically the case with young edge players. LT Overton was hardly used but did flash with two quick wins into the Texans backfield. They didn’t amount to much on the play, but those reps provided a tiny glimpse into his potential. Final grade: C The defense wasn’t a total disappointment this week. That’s a positive, right? Sure, they let up 30 points, including what could have been a game-winning touchdown. But they also kept Dallas in the game through the first half and allowed just 14 points in the second. How many games last season would have been 27-6 at the half? This is what progress looks like! I really wanted to give this defense a B- for their efforts against the Texans run game. It was by far their best effort of the season in that regard. Yes, the Texans have been pitiful while attempting to run the ball this season. But at the end of the day, you can only play who the schedule says to play. This unit did their job and made the Texans mostly one-dimensional throughout the day. The problem was that the Texans single dimension proved to be quite difficult for Dallas to slow down. The lack of a pass rush continues to baffle. While the defense finished with their best pass rushing day of the season, recording two sacks and five quarterback hits, it was not enough. The Texans offensive line has been extremely bad when protecting C.J. Stroud this year. This game could have very well been a coming out party for the Cowboys defensive front. Instead, it was just okay against a favorable matchup. The Cowboys secondary struggled on the day as well. DaRon Bland was in a close position for most of the day but had a difficult time finishing the play. Multiple big catches were made on the veteran cornerback, just out of his reach. Malik Hooker showed up at times, recording two pass breakups. Shavon Revel was on a limited snap count, as was Joey Porter Jr. What we did see of Porter Jr. should have Cowboys fans excited, however, allowing zero receptions on 19 snaps in coverage, being targeted just once. Dallas Cowboys CB Joey Porter Jr. played 24 of 52 possible defensive snaps in his debut with the team (46.2% playtime). This includes 19 snaps in coverage without allowing a single reception against just one target faced. (via @NextGenStats ) — RJ Ochoa (@rjochoa) October 4, 2026 There are plenty of reasons to be both optimistic and pessimistic about the Cowboys defense moving forward. We know the defense will continue to grow throughout the season. The question is when will it all come together, if ever? Can they actually generate a consistent pass rush at some point this year? How much will Joey Porter Jr. change the dynamics of this Cowboys secondary? For this week though, Christian Parker’s defense grades out at a solid C. The run defense was good, but the pass rush and secondary held them back. Their biggest positive was giving the offense time to get acclimated in Houston – something we didn’t see in many games last year. Next up, they’ve got a short week versus the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. This is another opportunity against a struggling opponent, including the backup rookie quarterback in Jalon Daniels. We’ll see if the Cowboys defense can ignite a spark this Thursday at AT&T Stadium.

title: ESPN insider offers 2 Detroit Lions trade target suggestion
summary: After being significant players in the trade talks for Joey Porter Jr.—but ultimately missing out—the Detroit Lions must go back to the drawing board if they want to upgrade their struggling secondary. Last week, we offered our own suggestions that Lions general manager Brad Holmes should consider. On Wednesday, ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler offered two more […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - SEPTEMBER 20: Kristian Fulton #8 of the Kansas City Chiefs lines up before a play during an NFL football game against the Indianapolis Colts at Arrowhead Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images After being significant players in the trade talks for Joey Porter Jr.—but ultimately missing out—the Detroit Lions must go back to the drawing board if they want to upgrade their struggling secondary. Last week, we offered our own suggestions that Lions general manager Brad Holmes should consider . On Wednesday, ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler offered two more trade targets Detroit should consider . “One potential option is Kansas City’s Kristian Fulton , who is in and out of the Chiefs’ lineup,” Fowler wrote. “He is owed real money — $5 million of his $9.75 million base salary is guaranteed — but perhaps the Chiefs and Lions could split the bill to facilitate a deal. Is it worth calling Pittsburgh for Jalen Ramsey ? Not sure he’s available, but the Lions’ defense seems far from settled.” Let’s handle these one by one. Fulton was the Titans’ second-round pick in 2020. After starting 37 games over four years in Tennessee, he signed a one-year deal with the Chargers in 2024. There, he produced a strong season: 51 tackles, seven passes defended, an interception, and a 68.9 PFF grade, ranking him 32nd out of 80 qualifying cornerbacks. Fulton parlayed that success into a two-year, $20 million deal with the Chiefs last year, but it turned out to be a failed year for him. A knee injury caused him to miss most of the offseason program, he dealt with a Week 2 ankle injury, and then essentially lost his job. He was a healthy scratch for about a third of the season, playing in just eight games and starting two. This year, Fulton has played more, but is not a full-time player. He’s logged 115 defensive snaps through four games, including a Week 3 contest against the Dolphins in which he did not play a single snap for reasons that are unclear. Despite the part-time gig, Fulton has held up well. He’s produced a 76.0 overall PFF grade and a 76.4 coverage grade. He’s been targeted eight times and allowed just four catches for 19 yards and an interception—though he does already have two penalties. KRISTIAN FULTON PICKS OFF DANIEL JONES 🤯 The Chiefs CB jumps the route and wins the ball for the interception 🔥 pic.twitter.com/xnqtquheTE — ClutchPoints (@ClutchPoints) September 21, 2026 Fulton’s usage is certainly peculiar, but it could suggest the Chiefs would be willing to move on. Fulton is a physical, handsy cornerback with average size (5-foot-11, 197 pounds) and acceptable speed (4.46 40-yard dash). As for Ramsey, his history of success is well documented. Since entering the league in 2016, he’s an eight-time Pro Bowler and three-time All-Pro. He’ll turn 32 later this month and certainly isn’t in the prime of his career, but he’s still producing at a strong level. From 2024-25, he produced 148 tackles, 19 pass breakups and three interceptions. But if you’re hoping that helps the Lions’ outside cornerback situation, he may not be the guy you’re looking for. Ramsey has mostly played as a nickel corner or safety with the Steelers this year—a transition he’s been making over the last two seasons. Could the Lions still use help at those positions? Absolutely. But if you want an upgrade on the perimeter, Ramsey is probably not the answer. As for financials, Ramsey wouldn’t come cheap. He’s currently sporting a $17.5 million salary—and that number jump to $19.7 in 2027 and $22 million in 2028—so it would likely be just a one-year rental for Detroit.

title: Detroit Lions scouting report: Arizona Cardinals better than their record shows
summary: Last week was called the “Petzing Bowl,” as Detroit Lions offensive coordinator Drew Petzing squared off against his brother, Dean Petzing, of the Carolina Panthers. This week, Drew Petzing plays his former team, the Arizona Cardinals, adding a little more drama to the matchup. After a Week 1 victory over the Los Angeles Chargers, the […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - OCTOBER 04: Elijah Higgins #84 of the Arizona Cardinals celebrates with teammates after scoring a touchdown against the New York Giants during the third quarter at MetLife Stadium on October 04, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Al Bello/Getty Images) | Getty Images Last week was called the “Petzing Bowl,” as Detroit Lions offensive coordinator Drew Petzing squared off against his brother, Dean Petzing, of the Carolina Panthers. This week, Drew Petzing plays his former team, the Arizona Cardinals, adding a little more drama to the matchup. After a Week 1 victory over the Los Angeles Chargers, the Cardinals have lost three straight, but don’t let the record fool you. This team has improved and has been playing good football, so don’t be surprised if this game turns into a shootout as both defenses struggle and the offenses keep it close. Let’s take a deep look at the Cardinals and how much they’ve changed ahead of Week 5. Arizona Cardinals 2025 season 3-14 record (4th in NFC West) 23rd in points for, 29th in points allowed Overall DVOA: 27th (24th on offense, 21st on defense) The Cardinals fell quickly in 2025. Quarterback Kyler Murray suffered a foot injury in Week 5, joining running back James Conner, who also suffered a foot injury in Week 3. Murray was replaced by veteran Jacoby Brissett, who did well under the circumstances he was in. Brissett threw for 3,366 yards, 23 touchdowns, and eight interceptions. He had to do a lot of the heavy lifting because he wasn’t getting help in the backfield, and he was constantly on his back, getting sacked 43 times; the Cardinals’ offensive line allowed 59 sacks overall, the fifth most in the NFL. The Cardinals had a lot of running backs start, with Michael Carter the most successful, leading the team with 333 yards and a touchdown. The team got a spark from Zonovan Knight, who ran for 269 yards and four touchdowns, but his season ended early as he suffered an ankle injury in Week 15 and was put on IR. With Brissett having to air it out, he leaned on tight end Trey McBride to carry the offense, finishing as the team’s leader in catches (126, setting an NFL record for tight ends) for 1,239 yards and 11 touchdowns. Wide receiver Michael Wilson had a breakout season, posting 78 catches for 1,006 yards and seven touchdowns. Second-year wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. finished with only 41 catches for 608 yards and four touchdowns. While the offense struggled, the defense tried its best to help. The Cardinals signed EDGE Josh Sweat in the offseason, and he was their best defender on the field, leading the team in sacks (12) and forced fumbles (four). He had a solid partner in crime in EDGE Calais Campbell, who, at 39, still got 6.5 sacks and was a presence on the defensive line. The secondary had some woes, but cornerback Denzel Burke led the team in interceptions (three) and pass deflections (11). Overall, once the wheels fell off the Cardinals offense, the rest of the season felt like a slow demise as they finished the year on a nine-game losing streak. Despite starting 2-0, the team finished 3-14, pushing their hopes to compete in the NFC to 2026. 2026 offseason Key additions: G Isaac Seumalo, RB Tyler Allgeier, DT Roy Lopez, WR Kendrick Bourne, LB Jack Gibbens, HC Mike LaFleur Key losses: QB Kyler Murray, S Jalen Thompson, DL Dalvin Tomlinson, DL Calais Campbell, OC Drew Petzing, HC Jonathan Gannon 2026 NFL Draft picks Round 1: RB Jeremiyah Love Round 2: G Chase Bisontis Round 3: QB Carson Beck Round 4: DT Kaleb Proctor Round 5: WR Reggie Virgil Round 6: LB Karson Sharar Round 7: OT Jayden Williams There was some drama for the Cardinals in the offseason. First, with the team falling flat on it’s face, head coach Jonathan Gannon was fired after finishing his career at 15-36 for three seasons. The Cardinals would move on and hire Los Angeles Rams offensive coordinator Mike LaFleur to be their new head coach. With Gannon gone, Petzing left Arizona to be the offensive coordinator for Detroit. Next, they moved on from Murray and had a contract standoff with Brissett, which ended with Brissett getting a reworked one-year deal for $21 million, $15.5 million guaranteed. The offensive line got some help at guard with the signing of Isaac Seumalo and the second-round draft pick of Chase Bisontis. With Conner still dealing with an injury, the team drafted running back Jeremiyah Love in the first round and signed Tyler Allgeier as a backup to add solid depth at the position. Arizona’s offensive shakeup didn’t stop there, as they signed wide receiver Kendrick Bourne and drafted wide receiver Reggie Virgil. Before signing Brissett to his reworked deal, the team drafted quarterback Carson Beck to help prepare for the future at the position. The defense took the biggest hit, losing safety Jalen Thompson and defensive linemen Dalvin Tomlinson and Campbell in free agency. Arizona countered those moves by signing defensive tackle Roy Lopez and drafting Kaleb Proctor. 2026 season thus far (1-3) Week 1: Defeated the Los Angeles Chargers 26-14 Week 2: Lost to Seattle Seahawks 31-7 Week 3: Lost to San Francisco 49ers 36-30 Week 4: Lost to New York Giants 36-24 Stats: 17th in points scored, 29th in points allowed Overall DVOA: 18th (12th on offense, 29th on defense, 4th on special teams) The season started with a bang for the Cardinals, who beat the Chargers on the road. They came down to earth the following week against the defending Super Bowl Champion Seattle Seahawks, losing by 24. Arizona didn’t let that loss deter them much, as they kept up with one of the three undefeated teams left in the NFL, the San Francisco 49ers, and almost pulled off another upset. Finally, against the New York Giants, they lost on the final play when Brissett attempted a fourth-down touchdown pass, but it was picked off and returned for a touchdown. Brissett has had a decent start to the season, throwing for 818 yards, six touchdowns, and four interceptions. Three of those interceptions came against the Giants, so he was doing well protecting the ball until last week. He’s been asked to carry the load as the running game hasn’t taken off yet, but it’s showing signs of improvement while Conner is still on the sidelines. Love leads the team in rushing yards with 223, averaging 4.1 yards per carry and a touchdown. Allgeier has 112 yards, averaging 3.5 yards per carry and a touchdown. The run game could certainly be better and ease some pressure off Brissett as he tries to carry the offense with his arm. The team’s current leading receiver is Wilson with 25 catches for 258 yards and a touchdown, but McBride is still Brissett’s go-to option. He leads the team in targets (46) and catches (33) for 242 yards and two touchdowns. Teams know McBride is the lifeblood of the passing game, and limiting his production forces Brissett to go elsewhere. Harrison got his first touchdown of the season against the Giants in Week 4, but he still has only five catches for 85 yards. While the offense has shown signs of life and moving the football, the defense hasn’t gotten that memo since Week 1. After the win over the Chargers, the Cardinals have allowed over 30 points in their last three games. Their last in the NFL in passing yards per attempt with 9.1, tied with the Lions and Washington Commanders for most passing touchdowns allowed (11), and have the second-highest QBR rating allowed at 114.9. Their best defensive player, safety Budda Baker, is everywhere for them this season, leading the team in sacks (1.5), tied for most interceptions (one), and tied for most pass deflections (three). He is the heartbeat of this defense and is playing what he is worth, while others haven’t been up to par. Sweat is off to a slow start (seven tackles and 1.0 sack) this season. Arizona’s defense is similar to Detroit’s, where opposing quarterbacks seem to have their way. Heck, they allowed Giants backup quarterback Jameis Winston to throw for…

title: 5 Lions vs. Cardinals thoughts after watching Arizona’s loss to Giants
summary: To help turn the page from the Detroit Lions’ previous game and set up expectations for the upcoming matchup, I spend some of my Tuesday watching the Lions’ next opponent’s most recent game. While it’s only a small snapshot of the team’s season, it provide a look at how they’re playing right now. I take […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - OCTOBER 04: Basil Okoye #99 of the New York Giants sacks Jacoby Brissett #7 of the Arizona Cardinals during the second quarter at MetLife Stadium on October 04, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Al Bello/Getty Images) | Getty Images To help turn the page from the Detroit Lions’ previous game and set up expectations for the upcoming matchup, I spend some of my Tuesday watching the Lions’ next opponent’s most recent game. While it’s only a small snapshot of the team’s season, it provide a look at how they’re playing right now . I take notes during the watch, then I compare those notes with some statistical outputs from the entire season to see if what I’m watching is congruent with how this team has been regularly playing or perhaps an outlier. So here are my thoughts on the 2026 Arizona Cardinals, and what it may mean for Sunday’s matchup with the Lions. Cardinals run game is only finding success on the perimeter… but that’s not good for Detroit This offseason, Arizona invested in their running game by signing RB Tyler Allgeier, drafting Jeremiyah Love, and signing guard Isaac Seumalo. But the overall impact of those additions have yet to be felt. The Cardinals sport a 3.9 yards per carry average (20th) and rank 13th in rush EPA. Against the Giants, they did finish with 123 rushing yards and 4.7 yards per carry, but almost none of that success was up the gut. However, stretch running plays to the outside were wildly successful, and if you look at their season-long numbers, they match what we saw in this game. They’re producing an impressive +0.26 EPA/rush outside the left tackle (fourth best) and +0.36 EPA/rush outside the right tackle (second) —while producing negative numbers pretty much everywhere else. Meanwhile, the Lions have been terrible at defending perimeter runs . They’re allowing +0.36 EPA/rush outside left tackle (second worst) and +0.17 EPA/rush outside right tackle (fifth). Detroit will need their defensive backs to play much more disciplined run defending on the edge. I’m looking at you, Christian Izien. Also, be on the look out for QB sneaks and tush pushes in short-yardage situations. Jacoby Brissett is 6-foot-4, 235 pounds, and it makes him very effective at that play. Jacoby Brissett crumbling under pressure I thought the Cardinals’ offensive line did a pretty good job when the Giants sent just four defenders in their pass rush. Considering New York has a pretty formidable front (albeit without Brian Burns in this game), I thought Brissett had fairly comfortable pockets. The Giants managed just a 17.6% pressure rate without blitzing, ranking 29th in Week 4. However, the Giants opted to crank up the blitz rate (51.3%, fifth), and the Cardinals didn’t have an answer. New York produced a 55.0% pressure rate when blitzing (eighth highest). Brissett is simply not a very good quarterback when the blitz is coming. He either checks down far too quickly (6.2 average depth of target, 27th out of 29 qualifying QBs) or is too risky with the football. Against the Giants, Brissett produced this statline under pressure: 6-of-12 for 53 yards, 1 TD, 2 INTs, and 50.3 passer rating. For the season, it’s even worse. Doesn’t matter whether the pressure is coming from a blitz or just a four-man runs: -0.32 EPA/dropback vs. blitz (25th out of 29) +0.01 EPA/dropback vs. no blitz (17th) -0.67 EPA/dropback vs. pressure (25th) +0.17 EPA/dropback vs. no pressure (17th) The Lions have been an abysmal defense in any situation, but particularly when blitzing. If Detroit can continue to generate pressure with just four—especially with Cardinals left tackle Paris Johnson Jr. now out for the year—I wouldn’t be surprised if they can generate some negative plays or turnovers. Cardinals defense found some pressure answers after rough start Going into the Giants game, the Cardinals’ defense was getting dragged publicly for their terrible pressure rate . For the season, the Cardinals still rank just 29th in pressure rate (30.3%). But against the Giants, they started to find some answers, and sacked Jameis Winston four times. The biggest solution was relatively simple: get more aggressive. The Cardinals upped their season-long blitz rate of 23.8% (23rd in NFL) to 30.3% and produced pressures on 40.0% of those blitzes (19th best). Detroit didn’t handle the blitz particularly well against the Panthers, but if they can, that is the key to beating this Cardinals defense. When Arizona cannot produce pressure, opposing quarterbacks are killing them. With no pressure, the Cardinals are allowed +0.50 EPA/pass (30th) and 9.6 yards per play (32nd). That’s because their primarily zone defense starts to fall apart when quarterbacks have time to process the coverage. With pressure, the Cardinals still aren’t great, but they’re better—ranking 29th in EPA/pass (-0.10) and 24th in yards per play (4.4). Run defense could give Detroit problems The Lions have run the ball very consistently this year, and the Cardinals present one of the tougher matchups thus far. They held the Giants to just 87 yards on 28 carries (3.1 YPC), and New York didn’t have a rush of over 9 yards. Now, New York has one of the worst rushing attacks in football through four weeks, ranking 24th in EPA and success rate, but for the season, the Cardinals have done a pretty good job. Arizona ranks fourth in rush EPA defense and 11th in success rate. Although the better rushing teams in football didn’t have a ton of issues against them (Seahawks: 162 yards, 4.1 YPC; 49ers: 140 yards, 6.1 YPC). The Lions aren’t ever going to go into a game expecting to abandon the run, but it’s clear to me that the bigger mismatch is through the air this week. Tight ends aren’t just about Trey McBride Yes, Trey McBride is arguably their biggest weapon in the passing game. He currently has 33 catches for 242 yards and two touchdowns. That is going to be a problem for a Lions defense that is surrendering 407 receiving yards (31st) and six touchdowns (32ng) to tight ends through four games. However, the Cardinals use 13 personnel (one running back, three tight ends) at a higher rate than everyone other than the Rams and Bills. That’s because they’ve got some dudes at that position beyond McBride. PFF’s highest-graded tight end in football through four weeks is actually Elijah Higgins (89.3 grade) because of his outstanding run blocking (77.0, second among TEs). Hunter Long has been their third tight end, and he’s also been a big asset in the running game (72.0 run blocking grade, 10th). Unfortunately, he was placed on IR this week, leaving Teagan Quitoriano to be the TE3 this week. Quitoriano has yet to play a game for the Cardinals this year, and his history suggests he’ll be a pretty significant downgrade.

title: Lions vs. Panthers Song of the Game: ‘War’ by Townland
summary: After every Detroit Lions game this season, someone on staff will select a song that incorporates the general feeling and vibes from the win or loss. By the end of the season, we will have a Spotify playlist that tells the full story of the 2026 Detroit Lions season. In Week 4, the Lions fell […]
full_text: Detroit Lions defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard reacts to a play against Washington Commanders during the second half at Northwest Stadium in Landover, Md. on Sunday, November 9, 2025. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co After every Detroit Lions game this season, someone on staff will select a song that incorporates the general feeling and vibes from the win or loss. By the end of the season, we will have a Spotify playlist that tells the full story of the 2026 Detroit Lions season. In Week 4, the Lions fell to the Carolina Panthers in humiliating fashion. Buckle up, we’re going to war. Week 4 Detroit Lions Song of the Game: ‘War’ by Townload So put up your dukes, we’re goin’ to war Ready the nukes, it’s DEFCON 4 When the Lions’ defense kicked off the season, they were declaring war on opposing offenses. Kelvin Sheppard’s initial vision of the defense was going HAM on quarterbacks. The defensive front was stunting, twisting, creating havoc. Detroit was sending aggressive blitzes and disguising their coverages. Unlike previous years, Detroit wanted to be assertive, unpredictable, and dictate the game on both sides of the ball. So armed with a 43.0% blitz rate, the Lions hoped to bring a nuclear attack to Tyler Shough and the Saints offense, and for the first half, it worked. But then the holes in the defense started to appear. Shough and the Saints came blazing back, and some uneasiness started to seep in. Was the first half a mirage, or the second? DEFCON 3 Assemble the troops, send in the corps To hell with détente, all I want is war We cranked up the panic meter after Josh Allen dismantled Sheppard’s defense from kickoff to handshakes. It shook us to our core, and it sent the Lions scrambling into their mini bye week. But also… it’s Josh Allen, wadda ya gonna do? Dan Campbell promised to come out of the break with a new plan, some new soldiers, and a reinvigorated spirit. It was far too early in the season to declare defeat. You better watch out, New York Jets. The Lions are ready to put a hurting on your obviously inferior squadron. You broke the rules of engagement and Rebuilt your ranks without so much as a thanks And now we’re at it hand-to-hand But I don’t want to fight anymore DEFCON 2 The Lions came out of the mini-bye with a fairly reformed defense (reformed does not necessarily mean better). They put down their fancy weapons of overly complicated blitzes to help their missile defense, shuffled their servicemen, and just tried to attack the Jets with plain, sound, hand-to-hand defense. Again, it worked until it didn’t. If it weren’t for a late sneak attack from Sergeant Clark, we may have already reached DEFCON 1. DEFCON 1 You’ve broken the sanctions that we swore But I reap what I sow ’cause all I know I reap what I sow ’cause all I know I reap what I sow ’cause all I’ve known is war Six months ago, Sheppard bragged of his offseason project . He spent all offseason watching the 2025 film and promised sweeping changes. Gone would be the explosive plays. The run defense would rise from the ashes of the Rams and Steelers games. He even watched tape from the best defenses to steal and incorporate their tactics . But a month into the season, those promises have already been properly dashed . Detroit’s defense has given up the highest rate of explosive plays (9.2%) , the second-highest rate of explosive run plays (15.5%), and the 12th-highest explosive pass rate (5.6%). And I fell for it all. I liked what they did at safety and defensive line this offseason to improve those units. I was intrigued by the new things they were doing in training camp. I was encouraged by how well they performed in practice. I should have known better. Ever since Ndamukong Suh chose Miami money over a hometown discount, this franchise has known nothing but pain and suffering on defense. For a dozen years, Detroit has been fighting a war just to climb to defensive mediocrity, and I fear it’s an endless one. If you want to relive previous Lions seasons, you can find the playlists we curated below: 2016 , 2017 , 2018 , 2019 , 2020 , 2021 , 2022 . And if you want to read previous versions of our Song of the Game columns, you can find those here .

title: What Detroit Lions fans want to know after Panthers loss
summary: Detroit Lions fans demand answers after the team fell to 2-2 on Sunday night. The Lions defense looked terrible again against the Carolina Panthers, and the offense remains disjointed and inconsistent. This week, coach Dan Campbell tried to provide some answers in a pair of media sessions. On Monday, he noted that while the defense […]
full_text: DETROIT,MICHIGAN-November27: A fan looks onto the field during an NFL football game between the Green Bay Packers and the Detroit Lions in Detroit, Michigan USA, on Sunday, November 23, 2025. (Photo by Amy Lemus/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images Detroit Lions fans demand answers after the team fell to 2-2 on Sunday night. The Lions defense looked terrible again against the Carolina Panthers, and the offense remains disjointed and inconsistent. This week, coach Dan Campbell tried to provide some answers in a pair of media sessions. On Monday, he noted that while the defense has a lot of issues—and they are digging to find solutions, including threatening more personnel changes—the offense needs to do a better job helping them out. Then, on Tuesday, a passionate Campbell offered more details about their search for answers, although he made sure he wasn’t going to give up everything to the public. We here at Pride of Detroit are not shackled by the same restrictions. We can assess the Lions’ issues on both sides of the ball, and offer our solutions publicly. There is no danger in us giving away game plans, nor do we have to worry about throwing specific players, coaches, or front office members under the bus. We can speak freely, where Campbell has to tread lightly. At the top of every month, we offer a MEGA mailbag just for our Pride of Detroit Direct subscribers. Our promise each month is that if you submit a question at the top of the month, we will answer it. As a result, these episodes are extremely long-lasting. This month, we answered over 60 questions, stretching our podcast to over 4.5 hours long. Here are the kinds of very thoughtful questions we answered for October’s edition of the Midweek Mailbag: If the whole idea behind press man is to disrupt timing and make the quarterback hold the ball longer, shouldn’t it pair really well with Detroit’s strong pass rush? The Lions’ linebackers seem to be struggling in pass coverage despite being a talented and expensive group. Do you think that’s because they’re built more for stopping the run, or is it a scheme or speed issue? If you had to divide the blame for the defense between personnel, scheme/play-calling, and player development/execution, how would you split it? Why is Nick Whiteside not getting a chance in all this shuffling? Would someone like Donte Jackson for the Chargers be a good trade candidate to look at? Was Kelvin Sheppard simply promoted too quickly? Do you think Dan Campbell’s loyalty to Sheppard is landing him in the hot seat job-wise? Could you see the Lions potentially letting go of defensive backs coach Deshea Townsend instead, similar to Aubrey Pleasant in 2022? What are your thoughts on the offense? It feels much improved, but still not quite as explosive as it was under Ben Johnson. Is there any chance that once we get into some division games, there’s more urgency and familiarity with scheme/ personnel? Could the Detroit Lions realistically trade Sam LaPorta? And could they net a defensive starter for him? Should the Lions adopt a trade-all strategy to restart and reload? Could the 2022 Lions’ midseason turnaround be replicated in 2026? How was Detroit’s offense not torching this defense in training camp? What makes good NFL centers so hard to find? That is quite literally just about 25 percent of the questions we got this week. If you want access to this month’s episode—plus weekly post-game videos, First Byte podcasts with a Lions opponent writer, and columns from Ty Schlater— you can sign up right here .

title: Dan Campbell gets passionate about offense ‘mediocrity,’ defensive fixes
summary: You could hear the passion in Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell’s voice on Tuesday morning as he faced another barrage of questions about the team’s lackluster start to the season—this time courtesy of John Jansen and Jim Costa, the hosts of 97.1 The Ticket’s morning show. As the interview progressed, Campbell got more and more […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - OCTOBER 31: Head coach Dan Campbell of the Detroit Lions yells from the sideline during the first quarter against the Philadelphia Eagles at Ford Field on October 31, 2021 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images You could hear the passion in Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell’s voice on Tuesday morning as he faced another barrage of questions about the team’s lackluster start to the season—this time courtesy of John Jansen and Jim Costa, the hosts of 97.1 The Ticket’s morning show. As the interview progressed, Campbell got more and more passionate with his answers, even admitting at the end of the interview that, “I am fired up, man. I am. I’m going forward, not backward.” Here’s a breakdown of the biggest takeaways from Campbell radio appearance. He’s not accepting mediocrity from the offense Campbell has received a bit of criticism for continuing to point to the offense needing to be better, when the Lions defense is arguably the worst in the league. On Tuesday, Campbell set the record straight, noting that the offense is too talented to accept what has been a relatively mediocre performance. When asked if the defense is putting too much pressure on the offense to be perfect, here was Campbell’s emphatic response “If you want to be great, they should want to score 35 points a game at a minimum. That’s what greatness is. That’s what they’re charged with. We’ve got plenty of weapons on offense, and if we’re going to accept mediocrity, then no. Then yeah, we can make all of the excuses in the world. But if we want to spit and sputter and be average, that’s one thing. “We’re not going to be average. We’re going to raise the floor on these guys. Man, we’re going to push them. “We’ve got too much offensively right now. Our quarterback’s too good. Our playmakers are too good. And we’ve got a young, hungry offensive line that’s got a ton of room to grow.” While the offense ranks in the top-10 or top-five in many stats, there are some significant areas to improve that could be described as average. In the running game, they’re just 16th in yards per rush (4.2) and 17th in rush EPA. They are also just 14th in third-down conversion rate (39.1%), and they’ve gone three-and-out t-17th most . Where the defense needs to improve most Jansen led off the interview asking Campbell if he could pick one thing for the defense to improve upon this week; what would it be? Campbell’s answer was a familiar one: “I want our guys to be where they’re supposed to be when they’re supposed to be there. We need to be on point. Our discipline has got to clean up,” Campbell said. This matches almost verbatim what Campbell said after Detroit’s loss against the Bills in Week 2. “Be where you’re supposed to be when you’re supposed to be there and do it with urgency across the board,” Campbell said after the Bills game. As to what is causing players to be out of place, Campbell listed a few things. For one, players are compensating for other players’ mistakes. Then, he believes the Lions are getting undisciplined with their eyes. “Probably boot(legs), dirty eyes on some stuff,” Campbell said. “The slam boots, the overs. That’s where we’re getting in trouble a little bit. It’s not really man or match coverage.” Ultimately, Campbell believes that despite the coverage issues, they have capable players in the building. “Inevitably, somebody’s going to be locked up one-on-one with no help, and you’ve got to win. And we have the guys that can win,” Campbell said. Looking for someone on defense to step up vs. tight ends We talked last week about the Lions’ struggles against tight ends . With one of the best tight ends in Trey McBride on deck for Cardinals week, the radio hosts asked Campbell how they plan to prepare. He gave a pretty unique answer: “You know what I want? I want somebody to come in tomorrow and say, ‘I want McBride.’ That’s what I want,” Campbell said. “I want to know who that’s going to be on our defense.” When asked who he’d prefer that player to be, he answered, “Anybody.” On defending Kelvin Sheppard Campbell noted that he certainly understands all the criticism of Lions defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard given the results and the statistics. But he backed Sheppard full-throatedly. “I believe in Kelvin Sheppard, and I believe we’ve got a lot of meat on the bone with this defense right now. Like I said, we’re going to continue to tweak. We’ve got more things that we can do with what we have here. There’s different calls, we’ve got to be more disciplined, and then we’re going to get some guys more opportunities to play here. We’re going to find the right recipe. “Here’s what I do know: At crunch time in that game the other day, at the end of the game with our defense on the field, we got two critical stops. That’s what I do know. So at the end of the day, after all of that, we had a chance to win that game and we couldn’t close it out. So I’ll take that.“ You can watch the entire interview below:

title: Week 5 power rankings: Detroit Lions fall, defense hammered by national media
summary: The Detroit Lions (2-2) have played in front of a national audience twice this season, and both primetime road games ended in losses. But the Lions didn’t just lose on the national stage; their defense was exposed, and regardless of what the offense was able to accomplish, it wasn’t nearly enough to overcome the hole […]
full_text: Detroit Lions head coach Dan Campbell talks to a referee after a play against Carolina Panthers during the first half at Bank of America Stadium in Charlotte on Sunday, Oct. 4, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions (2-2) have played in front of a national audience twice this season, and both primetime road games ended in losses. But the Lions didn’t just lose on the national stage; their defense was exposed, and regardless of what the offense was able to accomplish, it wasn’t nearly enough to overcome the hole the defense dug for them. As you might expect, getting beat up on a national stage brought negative national attention, and in this week’s power rankings, the Lions dropped on every analyst’s list, with each laying heavy blame on the defense for the team’s early-season struggles. Let’s take a closer look. The Athletic: 12 (Previous rank: 6) From Chad Graff and Josh Kendall : Concern level: Is this just what the defense is? This season, the Lions were supposed to be good enough to take advantage of an easy schedule. Instead, they’re coming off a loss because they couldn’t slow down Bryce Young, who threw for 329 yards and two touchdowns, and the vaunted(?) Panthers offense. The secondary is going to have nightmares about Tetairoa McMillan (14 receptions, 192 yards and two touchdowns). USA Today: 15 (Previous rank: 10) From Nate Davis : They’re certainly leaning on their stars, RB Jahmyr Gibbs with the most touches (102) in the league and WR Amon-Ra St. Brown (46) with the most targets. Gonna be hard to deviate from that formula given how bad the league’s most permissive defense has been … a state of affairs that seems unlikely to change any time soon. ESPN: 16 (Previous rank: 13) From ESPN Staff, excerpt from Eric Woodyard : Four words to describe the first four weeks: “Are you not entertained?” Like the famous line from the 2000 film “Gladiator,” you’re guaranteed some level of entertainment with this 2026 Lions team. Detroit scored at least 31 points in three of four games while also allowing 30 or more points in each. After the Week 3 win over the Jets, even coach Dan Campbell had to jokingly admit the Lions are worth the price of admission. “Tell you what, you’re coming to our games? You’re loving this now,” Campbell said. “I mean, these are exciting games. … Nobody’s leaving early. And that was the point. We’re not going to let anybody leave early this year.” NFL.com: 16 (Previous rank: 14) From Nick Shook : We saw on Sunday night that the key to beating the Lions is doing everything possible to bottle up Jahmyr Gibbs . A less effective Gibbs meant Jared Goff was forced to look elsewhere, leading to a couple of fruitless drives in the fourth quarter of a winnable game that ended in a loss . Detroit’s defense couldn’t limit Bryce Young, and its offense encountered a collection of potholes in crunch time. Sporting News: 18 (Previous rank: 11) From Vinnie Iyer : The Lions’ defense has been terrible for most of the season, save for Aidan Hutchinson. That’s putting too much on Jared Goff when Jahmyr Gibbs gets contained, like he was at Carolina. Sports Illustrated: 18 ( Previous rank: 14) From Connor Orr : A tip for Amon-Ra St. Brown: if you would like the quarterback of the Detroit Lions to come back on your podcast, you can’t blow him up for being a distant teammate on the first visit! Yahoo Sports: 19 (Previous rank: 13) From Frank Schwab : Detroit’s defense isn’t good enough to make the Lions scary to anyone. Detroit is allowing 423.8 yards per game, and no other NFL team is giving up more than 392.3. Detroit has allowed 127 points, most in the NFL. On Sunday against the Panthers, Tetairoa McMillan torched the secondary for 192 yards and two touchdowns on 14 catches. It’s bad enough that head coach Dan Campbell was asked afterward if defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard could be relieved of his duties. “I’m not talking about all that,” Campbell told the media after Sunday’s loss. “I’m talking about getting better right now, with what we’ve got, and that’s what we’re going to do. We’re going to find a way to get better with what we’ve got.” Campbell might not want to talk about it, but the Lions aren’t going anywhere with a defense this bad. CBS Sports: 20 (Previous rank: 12) From Pete Prisco : The defense is horrible. Even their good offense can’t overcome how bad they are right now.

title: Packers vs. Bears Week 5 TV Broadcast Map
summary: At the beginning of the 2026 NFL season, the Week 5 matchup between the Green Bay Packers and Chicago Bears looked set to be one of the biggest regular season games on the schedule. The two teams played three thrilling games in 2025, including a Wild Card matchup that went Chicago’s way after a late […]
full_text: CHICAGO, IL - DECEMBER 20: A FOX Sports broadcast camera operator prepares to perform their duty before a regular season game between the Green Bay Packers and the Chicago Bears on December 20, 2025, at Soldier Field in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Joseph Weiser/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images At the beginning of the 2026 NFL season, the Week 5 matchup between the Green Bay Packers and Chicago Bears looked set to be one of the biggest regular season games on the schedule. The two teams played three thrilling games in 2025, including a Wild Card matchup that went Chicago’s way after a late comeback. As a result, FOX claimed the game and seemed confident that it would remain one of the premier matchups this season, likely set to feature it as the Game of the Week in the late afternoon time slot. Fast-forward a few weeks and we find that this game has been flexed out of the featured time slot and back to an early kickoff at 12 Noon Central Time. The Packers stumbled out to a 2-2 start while Bears quarterback Caleb Williams is injured and will miss the game. Instead, FOX will feature 49ers-Seahawks, another divisional battle but one between two hot teams, as the main game in the late window instead. Still, a large portion of the USA will still be able to see Packers-Bears, particularly areas in the Central, Mountain, and Pacific time zones. Fans living in the Eastern time zone, however? You may be out of luck; Giants-Commanders and Bengals-Dolphins will take up much of the Eastern seaboard and Appalachia respectively, while Vikings-Saints claims a good portion of the southeast (as well as Minnesota and the Dakotas in the Central Time zone). Here’s this week’s broadcast map from 506sports.com, showing Packers-Bears in red: The Packers do get a bit of an upgrade on the commentators from their last two noon games, however. Both of those games (against the Jets and Saints) got FOX’s “C” team, both with Jonathan Vilma on the call as the color commentator. This week they get the “B” squad, which features Kenny Albert and Greg Olsen on the call. Albert is normally paired with Vilma, but he gets bumped up a notch again this week due to Olsen’s usual play-by-play partner, Joe Davis, covering baseball playoffs as FOX’s top commentator for that sport. Still, Olsen is a massive upgrade over Vilma for the ears of Packers fans this week. As usual, Packers fans whose home TV markets get other games will need to find alternate options to watch this week’s contest. NFL Sunday Ticket is the primary option, with the service still offering a 7-day free trial for new subscribers.

title: Green Bay Packers News: Zaire Franklin takes center stage
summary: You can count me among the people who were initially skeptical of the Zaire Franklin acquisition. Brian Gutekunst seems to have had an over-obsession with linebackers ever since De’Vondre Campbell’s out-of-nowhere All-Pro season in 2021, and his move to add Franklin as a replacement for Quay Walker, then reward him with a reworked contract, seemed […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - SEPTEMBER 24: Zaire Franklin #44 of the Green Bay Packers looks to defend during the first half of the NFL game against the Atlanta Falcons at Lambeau Field on September 24, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images You can count me among the people who were initially skeptical of the Zaire Franklin acquisition. Brian Gutekunst seems to have had an over-obsession with linebackers ever since De’Vondre Campbell’s out-of-nowhere All-Pro season in 2021, and his move to add Franklin as a replacement for Quay Walker, then reward him with a reworked contract, seemed like putting too many eggs in an aging and undersized basket. You can also count me as very glad that Gutekunst pulled the trigger on that move, especially since he only had to give up Colby Wooden, always a poor fit in Green Bay, to do it. Franklin has been a more-than-solid running mate for Edgerrin Cooper to this point. He’s played literally every snap of the Packers’ four games so far and he’s currently third on the team in tackles behind Evan Williams and Cooper. And Franklin donning the green dot had freed up Cooper to focus on doing Edgerrin Cooper things, always a plus when you’ve got a playmaker of his caliber. But now, Franklin is even more important to the Packers’ defense. With Cooper done for the year (and, unfortunately, at least part of 2027), Franklin’s contributions become all the more crucial to a defense that was just trying to get by until Micah Parsons came back. And with Parsons’ return apparently slightly slowed, someone’s going to have to make up for Cooper’s playmaking ability until the Packers’ best defender is back in the lineup. So yeah, I’m glad the Packers nabbed Zaire Franklin when they could. At least we’re not heading into a game against the Bears with Isaiah McDuffie and Ty’Ron Hopper as the starting linebackers. title: Packers Film Room: Random fun moments from a Week 4 win
summary: I know the vast majority of people have already moved past the Green Bay Packers’ Week 4 win over the Buccaneers and are looking forward to Week 5, but I’m not quite ready to do that yet, because there are still fun things to talk about from Week 4. So let’s take a couple minutes […]
full_text: Oct 4, 2026; Tampa, Florida, USA; Green Bay Packers running back Kaleb Johnson (26) runs with the ball past Tampa Bay Buccaneers linebacker Christian Rozeboom (52) at Raymond James Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Jonathan Dyer-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect I know the vast majority of people have already moved past the Green Bay Packers’ Week 4 win over the Buccaneers and are looking forward to Week 5, but I’m not quite ready to do that yet, because there are still fun things to talk about from Week 4. So let’s take a couple minutes and talk about them. Play 1: 3rd & 2, 10:32 remaining in the 1st quarter This is the Bo Melton [16] drop. It’s a real shame to refer to it that way, but I just assume it’s the way everyone will remember it so it’s a nice (sad?) little shorthand. The Packers are in 11 personnel (1 RB, 1 TE, 3 WR) in a 2×2 spread look. MarShawn Lloyd [32] is the running back, but, with the Bucs in a mugged-up look in the A gap, Lloyd is in the Sniffer role (aligned between the QB and the line). The Bucs are showing two-high safeties pre-snap with a lot of bodies up at the line. I mentioned the mugged-up A gap, but the slot defender over Matthew Golden [0] is inching towards the line, showing a blitz. Melton short-motions before the snap and Zyon McCollum [27] bumps over Golden. With Melton releasing out of the slot, that is showing Melton uncovered off the line. The Packers are running vertical routes – with Melton running right down the middle of the field – so Jordan Love [10] is going to check the safety movement post-snap but is already thinking about Melton as the first read on this play. At the snap, the slot defender drops into a hook zone (allowing Melton to fly by), the safeties are staying in their two-high look and one of the mugging linebackers is dropping off the line into zone, looking to pick up anything vertical from the slot. With Melton breaking vertical, the LB turns to run with him while the safeties turn to take a deep half of the field for each of them. It plays out like Tampa 2, with the LB covering the deep middle 3rd of the field. So that’s essentially Melton vs a linebacker, with that linebacker dropping from the middle of the line. Love checks the safeties, looks at the drops underneath and takes a shot on what is a very favorable match-up. Nice throw, but Melton just can’t hang on. Nice call. Good read. Good throw. Everything was perfect right up until the moment that it wasn’t. Still, in terms of everything that went into this, a fun call. I just wish it was a different outcome. Play 2: 2nd & 6, 6:32 remaining in the 1st quarter It’s been tough sledding for the Packers in the run game through the first few weeks of the season, but they broke off a couple explosive runs in this game so I wanted to look at them. Both of these runs come out of 13 personnel (1 RB, 3 TE, 1 WR). I mentioned this in my numbers breakdown after the game , but this was the heaviest usage of 13 personnel we’ve seen from the Packers this season, and it worked well for them. The Packers have all three of their TEs in-line. Jonnu Smith [18] is on the left, while Tucker Kraft [85] and Mark Redman [86] are in a YY Wing formation on the right. Redman goes in motion to the left pre-snap, which causes the linebackers to bump over. They snap the ball just before Redman crosses the center. On the left side of the line, Smith is kicking out the EMOL (End Man On the Line), Jordan Morgan [77] and Laken Tomlinson [72] are double-teaming the man over Morgan, and Sean Rhyan [75] takes a step to his left before turning back to block inside. Redman is working as a lead blocker for Chris Brooks. Everyone on the left side of the line does their job, with Redman taking on a LB in the hole. It looks like there’s a hole to the outside, but McCollum is lurking. Tomlinson comes off the double-team and releases over to give Redman a helping hand. Brooks does a nice job of seeing this and makes a great cut back inside, ultimately breaking through the line and picking up 27 yards. Play 3: 2nd & 5, 12:04 remaining in the 3rd quarter Another run out of 13, another explosive. Same formation as the last time, with the same players in the same spot. This time it’s a run to the right, and I really like how they get to it. Rhyan and Tomlinson work a double-team on the nose tackle to seal him inside. Travis Glover [79], Anthony Belton [71] and Tucker Kraft all block out, while Redman loops inside to work as a lead blocker. The key blocks up front are the Rhyan/Tomlinson double-team and the one-on-one with Glover. They all do their jobs wonderfully, creating a great running lane up front. Redman takes on the only other threat in the box. Kaleb Johnson [26] works behind that block and gets into the open field for a gain of 31. There are at least a dozen more plays I’d like to highlight here, but it’s late and I’m tired. Albums listened to: Zola Jesus – Conatus

title: Packers send Edgerrin Cooper to IR, call up Kristian Welch
summary: Once Monday’s medical exams took place, the Green Bay Packers moving linebacker Edgerrin Cooper to injured reserve was only a matter of when, not if, it would take place. The star linebacker tore his Achilles tendon in the Packers’ 17-14 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, and as of Tuesday afternoon he has officially gone […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - AUGUST 18: Kristian Welch #54 of the Green Bay Packers walks off of the field after an NFL football game against the Denver Broncos at Empower Field at Mile High on August 18, 2024 in Denver, CO. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images Once Monday’s medical exams took place, the Green Bay Packers moving linebacker Edgerrin Cooper to injured reserve was only a matter of when, not if, it would take place. The star linebacker tore his Achilles tendon in the Packers’ 17-14 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, and as of Tuesday afternoon he has officially gone to injured reserve. Taking Cooper’s place on the 53-man roster will be Kristian Welch, the veteran linebacker and special teams ace who has spent parts of the last few seasons with the Packers. Welch, who had been on the Packers’ practice squad over the first four weeks of the regular season, has been fully promoted to the 53-man roster to take Cooper’s place, both on the roster and in the linebacker room. Welch will almost certainly contribute immediately on special teams. The Packers used veteran backup linebacker Isaiah McDuffie heavily on teams over the first month of the season, but more reps for him on defense will mean that the team likely needs another body there. An injury to running back Chris Brooks, who also plays heavily on teams, could result in additional snaps for Welch on those units as well. Cooper started 17 of the Packers’ 18 games last year at linebacker, recording 118 total tackles with a half-sack, four pass breakups, two forced fumbles, and one fumble recovery. However, he had been emerging as an All-Pro candidate in 2026, his third NFL season, having recorded three sacks, an interception, and 30 tackles in just over 7 halves of football before his injury. Welch, meanwhile, has played one game for the Packers in 2026, as he was elevated to the gameday roster for the week 1 loss to Minnesota and made one special teams tackle. He played for the Packers in 2023 (14 games, 6 tackles), and 2025 (8 games, 3 tackles) as well, spending the second half of last season on the active roster before going on injured reserve himself in December. Meanwhile, with Brooks banged up, the Packers filled the vacant practice squad spot with a familiar running back. The team has brought back Damon Bankston, who spent a few weeks on the squad earlier this season. He rejoins Pierre Strong, Jr. on the squad, with Strong being a viable candidate to earn a gameday callup if Brooks’ injury is significant enough to keep him out of the lineup this weekend.

title: Packers’ slow pace is another sign of offensive struggles
summary: We’ve been tracking the Packers’ pace of play for a while. I wrote about it a couple of times last year, including this midseason piece, and our Paul Noonan was on the case all the way back in 2020. Generally speaking, under Matt LaFleur the Packers have run a pretty slow-paced offense, snapping the ball […]
full_text: TAMPA, FLORIDA - OCTOBER 4: Quarterback Jordan Love #10 of the Green Bay Packers during warmups prior to their game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Raymond James Stadium on October 4, 2026 in Tampa, Florida. (Photo by Parker S. Freedman/Getty Images) | Getty Images We’ve been tracking the Packers’ pace of play for a while. I wrote about it a couple of times last year, including this midseason piece , and our Paul Noonan was on the case all the way back in 2020 . Generally speaking, under Matt LaFleur the Packers have run a pretty slow-paced offense, snapping the ball relatively few times per game even as the rest of the league runs fewer and fewer plays right along with them. There are many reasons for the glacially slow pace in Green Bay and across the league. Motion and pre-snap shifts were once an occasional tool but now feature into virtually every offensive play. Teams soak up more and more of the play clock trying to force the defense into tipping its hand, all the while players are moving around like clockwork getting into just the right spot before the quarterback finally agrees to get things started. But this year, the bottom has truly fallen out in Green Bay, and it’s not actually for any of the above reasons. It’s because the Packers just can’t stay on the field on offense. The Packers have averaged just 58.75 plays per game across their first four games, more than three full plays below the league average of 61.79. The Packers are averaging just 5.5 plays per drive (26th most in the league and the fewest of the Matt LaFleur era) and are tied for sixth in the league with 12 three-and-out drives . I don’t intend to argue here that “playing fast” or running more plays would fix the Packers’ offense, but this is just pointing out that the Packers’ relatively few plays per game is a symptom of how badly the offense is playing overall. The Packers’ best offensive performance — to a point — came in Week 1, when the Packers really only had two of their first eight drives stall out before their failed fourth down attempt turned things around for the Vikings. I think we can largely set that game aside. But in Week 2, the Packers’ opened the game with three straight three-and-out drives and ran no more than three offensive plays on five of their first seven possessions. Their eighth drive ended with a fumble on the first play. It’s easy to see how they found themselves in a hole against the Jets. Week 3 was much the same. The Packers had four straight drives in the first half that ended after four plays or fewer, and the Falcons took advantage of a gassed Packers defense by reeling off four consecutive drives of their own where they never ran fewer than seven plays. They scored two touchdowns and a field goal in the process, taking advantage of a gassed Packers defense. The Packers finally cleaned things up a bit in Week 4, where they never had consecutive three-and-out drives at any point. Unsurprisingly, this was one of their better offensive games, which doesn’t say much, but we’ll take what we can get. Again, this isn’t meant as an argument that the Packers should just find a way to run more plays, but rather another data point for how the offense has struggled to this point. When we start seeing more sustained drives and fewer dead-on-arrival possessions, we’ll know things are heading in the right direction. Until then, the Packers’ offense is going to be spending more time on the sideline than anyone would like.
