title: Packers Film Room: Green Bay’s Week 4 touchdowns
summary: The Green Bay Packers got a Christian Watson touchdown for three straight weeks, so I just kind of assumed that was going to keep happening all year. We didn’t get a Watson TD in the team’s week 4 win over the Buccaneers, but we did get a couple other scores I wanted to dig into […]
full_text: TAMPA, FL - OCTOBER 04: Green Bay Packers Quarterback Jordan Love (10) throws a pass during the regular season game between the Green Bay Packers and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on October 04, 2026 at Raymond James Stadium in Tampa, Florida.(Photo by Cliff Welch/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Green Bay Packers got a Christian Watson touchdown for three straight weeks, so I just kind of assumed that was going to keep happening all year. We didn’t get a Watson TD in the team’s week 4 win over the Buccaneers, but we did get a couple other scores I wanted to dig into a bit, so here we go. Play 1: 4th & 2, 12:58 remaining in the 2nd quarter The Packers are in 11 personnel (1 RB, 1 TE, 3 WR) at the goal line. They’re in a Nub formation (3 receivers to one side, an in-line TE on the other side), with a bunch formation on the right. They start with Sky Moore [23] at the point, Matthew Golden [0] on the inside and Christian Watson [9] on the outside. Golden shifts outside before the snap and the coverage bumps as a result. At the snap, Moore takes off on a shallow drag, Watson releases vertically (veering outside initially) and Golden takes a step in to follow Watson. At this point, it looks like a version of Shield, a concept the Packers like in this area of the field. On this concept, Watson would work as the “Shield” for Golden, who would be running a Now slant underneath him, off Watson’s hip. It can be incredibly difficult for the defense to stop this if run correctly. Keionte Scott [22] is the inside defender over the bunch and he’s looking for this on the release. He jumps under Watson and is looking to pick up Golden on the slant. Instead, Golden runs a quick out. With Scott on the inside shoulder, Jordan Love [10] has room to put this ball. He throws over Scott in the end zone, and Golden goes up and makes a nice catch. Play 2: 2nd & 2, 10:39 remaining in the 3rd quarter Once again down at the goal line, the Packers come out in 12 personnel (1 RB, 2 TE, 2 WR) in a balanced formation (under center, single back aligned behind the QB, a TE in-line on each side, a WR split wide to each side). Before the snap, they shift Watson into an insert position (under the line, between the TE and the tackle). This is a way to give a little more heft to the running game, so the Bucs are looking for a run to the right side. Over the past couple of years, that insert position has seen wide receivers releasing through the line on vertical routes at an increasing rate. This year, we’ve seen a lot of teams score TDs off of this. In fact, we saw Watson score 2 TDs off of this ( Week 1 and Week 3 ). In both of those we’ve seen Watson release through the line and to a corner route, and Love found him in the end zone. They’re looking for the same thing here, but Zyon McCollum [27] is looking for it as well, staying home in the deep part of the field. Unfortunately for the Bucs, there is another option. Tucker Kraft [85] is the TE to the play side. He gives a cursory block to Anthony Nelson [98], then releases to the flat. With McCollum dropping back to pick up Watson, there’s no on in the flat. Tykee Smith [23] is over Watson and sprints to pick up Kraft, but there’s only so much he can do. Nelson comes off the block from Kraft and is baring down on Love, but Love is able to loft this ball over the top of Nelson and into the hands of Kraft at the front pylon. I also really like that Arches concept on the backside between Golden and Mark Redman [86]. Normally you see that from a tighter split (or that Arches route coming from the backfield), but the delayed route from Redman makes this work. Definitely one to look out for in the future. Albums listened to: Stevie Wonder – Songs in the Key of Life ; Julia Jacklin – The Gem ; Talk Talk – Spirit of Eden ; The Smile – Wall of Eyes

title: Predict the Packers’ record in NFC North games in 2026
summary: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Packers fans and fans across the country. In Week 5, the Green Bay Packers will play their second game within the NFC North division this season. The first such game did not go […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - DECEMBER 07: Keisean Nixon #25 of the Green Bay Packers catches an interception during the fourth quarter against the Chicago Bears at Lambeau Field on December 07, 2025 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by John Fisher/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Packers fans and fans across the country. In Week 5, the Green Bay Packers will play their second game within the NFC North division this season. The first such game did not go well for the Packers, as they continued last season’s trend of blowing big leads. A Week 1 visit to Minnesota saw Green Bay take a 22-10 lead late in the third quarter before allowing 29 straight points as the Vikings pulled away for a commanding victory. The Packers now sit 0-1 in their divisional games with five remaining, and next up are the Chicago Bears, who come into Lambeau Field on Sunday afternoon. Chicago will be starting backup quarterback Tyson Bagent in that game, but Bagent and third stringer Case Keenum have each led the Bears to wins over the past two weeks. If Green Bay can find a way to win on Sunday, it would significantly shake up the perceived balance of power in the NFC North. The Packers are 2-2 overall right now, just one game behind the 3-1 Bears for second in the division, but a Green Bay victory would draw the two teams level and it would give Green Bay an important head-to-head tiebreaker. Two weeks after this upcoming game, the Packers will wrap up the first round of matchups with a trip to Detroit in Week 7. They then host the Vikings in Week 10 before heading back to Chicago on Christmas Day in Week 16 and concluding the season at home against the Lions. Those are five big opportunities still ahead to make a big statement in the division. With the Packers’ first game in their “Rivalries” uniform on deck this week, we want to know how Packers fans think the team will end up faring in divisional games when all is said and done. Do they find a way to get to .500 on the season by going 3-2 in the final five divisional games? Could they sweep one or two of their other rivals and actually get above .500? Last season, the Packers swept the Lions, but split with the Vikings and Bears in the regular season to finish with a 4-2 divisional record. The year before, however, they managed to go 11-6 despite a brutal 1-5 result in the NFC North. So which will it be this year? Let us know in the poll and the comments below. title: Green Bay Packers News: What do the Packers do without Edgerrin Cooper?
summary: How do you replace Edgerrin Cooper? You don’t. There, the intro for this edition of our Tuesday links column is done! We’ve solved the Packers’ post-Cooper linebacker dilemma by identifying that there is no solution. But seriously, I’m always a little frustrated (annoyed? vexed?) by the intractable situation that arises whenever the Packers lose a […]
full_text: TAMPA, FLORIDA - OCTOBER 4: Linebacker Edgerrin Cooper #56 of the Green Bay Packers has to be carted off the field in the third quarter against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Raymond James Stadium on October 4, 2026 in Tampa, Florida. (Photo by Parker S. Freedman/Getty Images) | Getty Images How do you replace Edgerrin Cooper? You don’t. There, the intro for this edition of our Tuesday links column is done! We’ve solved the Packers’ post-Cooper linebacker dilemma by identifying that there is no solution. But seriously, I’m always a little frustrated (annoyed? vexed?) by the intractable situation that arises whenever the Packers lose a key player. It’s both impossible to come up with a solution, because certain players certainly approach irreplaceability, and an essential question, because you’re not going to just play with 10 players on the field because one guy suddenly finds himself short an Achilles tendon. You’re clearly never going to find a one-to-one replacement for Edgerrin Cooper. His stat line from Sunday (nine tackles, a sack, and an interception) has only been produced by a Packers player three other times this century (by Xavier McKinney in 2025, Charles Woodson in 2009, and Nate Wayne in 2001). Players like Edgerrin Cooper don’t grow on trees, and the truly annoying part is that he appeared to only be getting better. But you need a solution. What’s it going to be? It’s not leaning more heavily on Zaire Franklin; his workload is big enough already and his limitations as an undersized linebacker on the wrong side of 30 are apparent. It’s not turning to Isaiah McDuffie; we’ve seen that movie before. It’s not Ty’Ron Hopper; if he were any good, we’d have seen it by now. So what’s it going to be? How do you keep getting plays from your defense while offsetting the loss of one of your very best players? Throw it on the pile, because this is just another question that will define the Packers’ season. There may not be a satisfying answer, but the Packers are obligated to try to find one. title: Houston Texans NFL Power Rankings: Week 5
summary: Is this it for the Houston Texans in 2026? Is this the unceremonious closing of their Super Bowl window? These may be questions you find easy to answer now, but were you expecting that to happen so early into this season? Some believe that’s it’s hard to get a read on any NFL teams until […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - OCTOBER 04: Kamari Lassiter #3 of the Houston Texans reacts after a penalty in the second half against the Dallas Cowboys at Reliant Stadium on October 04, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Tim Warner/Getty Images) | Getty Images Is this it for the Houston Texans in 2026? Is this the unceremonious closing of their Super Bowl window? These may be questions you find easy to answer now, but were you expecting that to happen so early into this season? Some believe that’s it’s hard to get a read on any NFL teams until a quarter of the way into the season. Of course, you can often glean which teams are truly great and which are awful right away, but the majority of teams fall between those two extremes and require a sample size of a few games to figure out. Now that we’re four games into the regular season, it’s a bit easier to determine which teams are trending in the right and wrong direction…and Houston is going in about as wrong of a direction as you could possibly imagine. Four losses in a row is a new low for this new era of Texans football, the last time it occurred was the 2020 season and resulted in head coach/general manager Bill O’Brien being fired when he was arguably at the peak of his powers within the organization. Unlike 2020, however, there’s a head-spinning mishmash of newfound problems that haunt the 2026 Texans: the insistent, exhausting struggling of the offensive line and rushing attack now in their third year of failing to improve, the surprising development of significantly worse defensive coverage (partially caused by playing more zone rather than man outside the numbers), and, of course, the injuries. The injuries to the offensive line, wide receiver, and linebacker position groups have been truly disastrous to the team’s cohesion, and the depth of the roster has not been able to pick up the slack in the way I’m sure general manager Nick Caserio intended. So, what does this all mean for the Texans’ spot on the power rankings? It means that they’re going down, way down, and it will require a miracle for Houston to break into the top half of the list by season’s end. The only NFL team to go 0-4 and still make the playoffs was the 1992 San Diego Chargers, and after last month’s showing, I strongly doubt any pundits will be betting on the Houston Texans from repeating that remarkable feat. Here’s where the Houston Texans are ranked following their 34-30 loss to the Dallas Cowboys: NFL.COM : 23. Houston Texans (0-4) I think it’s safe to remove the “elite” tag from the Texans’ defense. For a second straight week, C.J. Stroud gave Houston a late lead, and the defense failed to protect it. Kamari Lassiter had an especially terrible day, giving up eight receptions for 136 yards on 11 targets as the closest defender, per Next Gen Stats. Houston’s defense didn’t generate organic pressure, resorting to blitzes against a quarterback ( Dak Prescott ) you certainly should not blitz often. The Texans paid the price and have wasted a rather strong stretch from Stroud, who is no longer the problem in Houston. – Nick Shook ESPN: 24. Houston Texans (0-4) Week 4 result: Lost to the Cowboys 34-30 Week 4 ranking: 21 Four words to describe the first four weeks: Pass defense is struggling. The Texans’ pass defense has fallen off a cliff in 2026. Last season, Houston was fifth in passing yards allowed (179 per game). So far in 2026, it’s 28th (260). For a team with three Pro Bowlers in the secondary, that’s inexcusable. There are a bunch of reasons, but a noteworthy one is that Houston hasn’t pressed as much as last season. The Texans have the second-lowest press rate (25%), per ESPN Research, compared to the 12th highest in 2025 (56%). That has been a little confusing, as All-Pro cornerback Derek Stingley Jr . and Pro Bowl corner Kamari Lassiter are best when pressing – DJ Bien-Aime SPORTS ILLUSTRATED: 20. Houston Texans (0–4) Last week’s ranking: No. 16 Last week’s result: lost to Cowboys, 34–30 This week: at Titans Of the teams whose seasons are theoretically dead in the water, Houston provides the faintest glimmer of hope. Braden Smith, Tank Dell and Kayden McDonald are on the way, the Titans are up next on the schedule and 1–4 looks far better (with three examples of playoff teams in the last 25 years, by the way). – Conor Orr BLEACHER REPORT: 28. Houston Texans (0-4) Last Week: 27 Week 4 Result: Lost vs. Dallas 34-30 The Houston Texans understand what it means to start poorly then rally to earn a postseason appearance. However, the team has never started 0-4 and made the playoffs. Only one team in NFL history has. What makes Houston’s situation particularly concerning is the team could rely on its defense last season. This year is a different story. Houston went from fielding the league’s best defense to sitting outside of the Top 20. Houston currently ranks among the bottom five pass defenses. Derek Stingley Jr. and the Texans’ secondary couldn’t slow CeeDee Lamb. Instead, Lamb set a new Dallas Cowboys franchise record Sunday with 17 receptions in a single game. Ironically, Houston’s offense was the bigger concern entering the 2026 campaign. It’s currently ranked sixth overall. – Brent Sobleski CBS SPORTS; 26. Texans (0-4) (Last Week: 27) They’ve made the playoffs after opening 0-3. But this year it’s 0-4. Can they climb out from that hole to make the playoffs? Good luck. – Pete Prisco USA TODAY: 27. Houston Texans (25): Even if an 0-4 outfit wanted to wave the white flag , the contracts of players like DE Danielle Hunter and WR Nico Collins are basically untradeable due to their salary cap ramifications. – Nate Davis YAHOO! SPORTS: 26. Houston Texans (0-4, LW: 24) With 2:23 left on Sunday, the Texans scored to take a 30-27 lead. A defense that was expected to be one of the best in the NFL could win the game with one stop, or at least make sure the game went to overtime by holding Dallas to a field goal. The Cowboys went downfield and scored a touchdown. Dallas has a good offense but Houston was supposed to have a good defense. The Texans don’t. They are surprisingly average: 14th in DVOA after Sunday’s games and 26th in EPA ( expected points added ) allowed per play. Defensive dominance can vary more season to season than offensive excellence, but it’s still surprising that the Texans are winless and a middle-of-the-road defense is a big reason for that. “It sucks, because we know we’re the ones out there on the field,” Texans cornerback Derek Stingley Jr. said, via the Houston Chronicle . “The coaches put us in the right position to win and we’ve got to do it. They can’t do it, we’ve got to do it. We’ve got great coaches, we’ve got great everybody. We’ve got to go out there and do our job.” – Frank Schwab THE ATHLETIC 24. Houston Texans (0-4) Last week: 22 Sunday: Lost to Cowboys 34-30 Concern level: Sky-high This was supposed to be a team that could compete for the Super Bowl in a wide-open AFC. Instead, a defense that we thought had a chance to be an all-time great has looked awfully mediocre through the first four weeks. It’s the main reason for the Texans’ winless start. Up next: at Titans, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET – Chad Graff & Josh Kendall PRO FOOTBALL TALK: 24. Texans (No. 17; 0-4): Where did the Houston defense go? – Mike Florio Average Ranking: 24.67 (Last Week: 22.56) Yeah, ouch. The Texans started the season as one of the Super Bowl favorites in the AFC, and now they’ll be lucky to dig themselves out of the 20s by January. What are the chances that they even mount a comeback? Well, like SI’s Conor Orr stated, they’ll be getting quality players back from injury soon, and the 0-4 Tennessee Titans (the same team that kickstarted Houston’s comeback last year) are up next. By comparison, that 1992 0-4 Chargers team that made the playoffs was led by QB Stan Humphries, WR Anthony Miller, RBs Ronnie Harmon, Marion Butts, (current Chiefs offensive coordinator) Eric Bienemy on offense, and DE Leslie O’Neal and LB Junior Seau on…

title: Houston Texans Defense: Serious Problem?
summary: The Houston Texans entered the 2026 season with sky-high expectations after their dominant display the season prior. They are pretty much stacked at all three levels of the defense, but somehow, things have not looked the way they used to. Regression is always possible in the NFL, but the drop-off from one year to the […]
full_text: The Houston Texans entered the 2026 season with sky-high expectations after their dominant display the season prior. They are pretty much stacked at all three levels of the defense, but somehow, things have not looked the way they used to. Regression is always possible in the NFL, but the drop-off from one year to the next, especially without losing much talent, has been troublesome. If you look back at the start of last season, the Texans’ defense also started somewhat slow and did not immediately become the dominant unit we eventually saw. The offense could not get much of anything going, and the defense was doing everything it could to keep Houston in games. This year, it has been almost the complete opposite. Houston’s offense has looked far better when fully healthy. The Texans have put up 30 points per game when their best wide receiver, Nico Collins, has been on the field. He missed two games this season, and the offense struggled tremendously without him, but that is a story for a different day. The reality of the situation is that quarterback C.J. Stroud gave the Texans a late fourth-quarter lead in three of their first four games. In each of those situations, the defense had an opportunity to get a stop and close out the game, but they were unable to do so. That is a major reason why this team is sitting at 0-4. Defensively, the Texans have immense talent, and there is no questioning that. The issue is that it feels like the players are not always being put in the best situations to succeed, especially when it comes to the scheme in certain situations. This is a defense loaded with players who have already proven they can play at an elite level. When a unit this talented continues to struggle in crucial moments, eventually you have to look beyond the players themselves and figure out what needs to change. In order for Houston to have any chance of turning this season around, the defense simply has to be better. The good news is that there is plenty of reason to believe that will happen. There is far too much talent on this roster for this unit to continue playing at this level. Defensive end Will Anderson Jr. is already having a Defensive Player of the Year-caliber season and has been practically unstoppable through the first four games. He has established himself as the anchor of this defense and continues to make an impact on a weekly basis. The Texans now need the rest of the defense to follow his lead. Starting 0-4 is obviously far from ideal, and Houston has put itself in a difficult position moving forward. However, this does not feel like a team that is completely lost. They have been in position to win several of these games and have simply failed to finish them. They are close. Now, they have to prove that being close can eventually turn into winning football games.
author: Nickschwager

title: Value of Things: Life on the hot seat
summary: Last week I started the whole notion of the stages of suck and that continues unabated as the Texans drop to 0-4 for the first time in franchise history. Even the David Culley experience managed a victory in week one. Since this is unchartered waters it is impossible to see everyone in the key spots […]
full_text: Last week I started the whole notion of the stages of suck and that continues unabated as the Texans drop to 0-4 for the first time in franchise history. Even the David Culley experience managed a victory in week one. Since this is unchartered waters it is impossible to see everyone in the key spots making it out alive. So, the question is exactly how warm is everyone’s seat getting? Naturally, this is just one observer’s opinion. People are free to flood the comments with their own. However, let’s start on top. Nick Caserio These reports come out on Wednesday for a reason. Ultimately, we want to avoid making irrational decisions. Someone wise once said that perfect is the enemy of good. What they meant is that we can discard good way too easily in the search of perfect. The perfect general manager doesn’t exist. The hot name this week will be on the chopping block next month. Howie Roseman is a perfect example. One or two years ago he was the best general manager in sports. Now, Eagles fans are looking at him with side eye. On balance, Caserio has taken this organization from the land of Bill O’Brien hell into constant competitiveness the last three years. Even three of these four games where down to the final possession. Yes, there are cracks in the veneer. Everyone focuses on the offensive line for obvious reasons, but there are other free agency misses as well. There have been draft misses as well. I would challenge any detractor to look at the records for any of the other general managers and name me ten better ones. It would be a difficult task. However, the GM’s job is about much more than players. The coaching staff has his fingerprints all over it. In particular, the offensive coordinator and offensive line coach appear to be buddy hires. Interesting how those two units are coming under more scrutiny than any of the others. If we are looking at this from the Goldilocks zone of cold, warm, and hot then we would have to put Caserio in the warm category. I can’t see much of a case for firing him at this moment, but once this debacle is over he will be put on notice to get coaching hires and the offensive line right. Another year of this and he could be out. Seat: Warm DeMeco Ryans Like with Caserio one should consider whether you can do better. That is a very reasonable question. For some, simply having an offense first coach is always preferable and that is more than fair. However, it is fair to ask what Ryans has done to deserve the axe. It is only one man’s opinion, but I see him as 2010 Gary Kubiask. Kubiak was a gifted offensive mind and had one of the more prolific offenses in the NFL at the time. In fact, the Texans offense has never been better than it was in 2010. He just couldn’t figure out the defensive side of the ball. The McNairs stepped in and hired Wade Phillips and forced him on Kubiak. It might be that time for Ryans. 2010 was year four for Kubiak and 2026 is year four for Ryans. My personal view is that Caley was selected for him. He failed when he brought in his own guy. So, that means Hannah McNair needs to come to the rescue and hire someone for Caserio and Ryans. The decision needs to be taken out of their hands. No more buddy hires. The Colts game was rife with clock management issues, but those were cleaned up this week. He is growing as a football coach and he should be here for the long haul. Obviously consecutive losing seasons would change the calculus on that, but I see him on the Kubiak track. He will recover with a better offensive staff and hopefully Stroud will stay healthier than Matt Schaub. Seat: Cold Nick Caley The life of a teacher can be cruel. Teachers are usually put into three different buckets. There are those that are pros and we just leave them alone and let them do their thing. There are those that show promise, but have areas where they can definitely grow. We keep them around and offer them training and support until they figure out what they need to figure out. Then there are those that are lost causes. You bide your time and get rid of them when you can. I have been all three in my teaching career. The differences were based on the situation. I am built to do specific things well and when allowed to do those things I will be great. There are other things I don’t do well and situations where I will struggle. So, I get Nick Caley more than most people. Caley isn’t an idiot. He is just in a bad situation for him and his skill set. Sometimes it is a location thing. Sometimes it is a question of what is being asked. Sometimes it is a question of the tools that are given to him. Either way, we are beyond the stage of hoping and working towards growth. I have little doubt that Caley could potentially succeed in a different situation. He just isn’t the right guy for this job. Even in his good weeks there are too many instances where he is overmatched. The hook and lateral play in the fourth quarter was a moment of brilliance in a sea of mediocrity. There just aren’t enough of those moments to make up for the mediocrity. Looking back he probably should have been one and done, but they wanted to give him a chance to grow and I can’t fault them for that. It just didn’t work. Seat: Scalding Hot

(Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images According to head coach Shane Steichen, the Indianapolis Colts are opening the 21-day practice window for backup tight end Will Mallory, who’s coming back from a thumb injury (via FOX59/CBS4’s Mike Chappell): On IR with thumb injury. https://t.co/de8Fde8lRg — Mike Chappell (@mchappell51) October 7, 2026 It means that Mallory will be eligible to be activated off the team’s injured reserve within the next three weeks. If he’s not activated during that same span, he will remain on injured reserve for the remainder of the 2026 season. The Colts’ 4th-year tight end suffered the thumb injury during a joint training camp practice against the Atlanta Falcons on August 20th. Mallory did not play in the team’s following two preseason games because of the injury. He was later placed on injured reserve with a designation to return as part of the Colts’ final 53 man roster cut maneuvers on August 31st. Indianapolis currently has a crowded tight end room with Tyler Warren, veteran Mo Alie-Cox, and Drew Ogletree, so the Colts would have to carry four tight ends on their 53-man active roster with Mallory’s potential upcoming activation. The former 2023 5th round pick of the Colts stood out in this year’s preseason opener against the New England Patriots on the road, catching a team-leading 6 receptions for 80 total receiving yards. He’s not a candidate to be waived and re-signed to the Colts practice squad, as there’d be a serious chance that another NFL team would poach him during that process.

title: Alec Pierce’s prolonged absence is killing the Colts
summary: The Indianapolis Colts are facing a bit of a crisis at the wide receiver position. Michael Pittman Jr. was traded this offseason. He didn’t seem to have his best stuff anymore, but that one still hurt. Alec Pierce was tabbed to be the next man to take over the reins as the number one receiver. […]
full_text: London, United Kingdom - October 4: Daniel Jones of Indianapolis Colts in action during the Indianapolis Colts and Washington Commanders match between Indianapolis Colts and Washington Commanders at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on October 4, 2026 in London, United Kingdom. (Photo by Vince Mignott/DeFodi Images/DeFodi via Getty Images) | DeFodi Images via Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts are facing a bit of a crisis at the wide receiver position. Michael Pittman Jr. was traded this offseason. He didn’t seem to have his best stuff anymore, but that one still hurt. Alec Pierce was tabbed to be the next man to take over the reins as the number one receiver. Since cashing his check, we have hardly seen him on the field. The Colts are feeling the effects. Statistically, Daniel Jones had his worst quarter and a half against the Commanders. There was pressure, but his attempts were the shortest in the league at 3.8 per play. Going 19/34 for only 143 yards and multiple turnovers proves Jones is struggling. Josh Downs is the twitchy man the Colts need underneath, but no one can take the top off the defense. Laquon Treadwell has been the Colts’ best downfield threat. No offense to Treadwell, but he isn’t going to cut it. Pierce was the deep threat. Last year, he added more routes and became more of a well-rounded receiver. That made his deep threat even more lethal. Jones averaged over 8 yards per attempt last year with Pierce in the fold. Not only would Pierce provide an option for a deep shot, he also opened the rest of the field by taking defenders with him away from the line of scrimmage. His presence on the outside changes everything. Another heel injury is crippling the Colts. Alec Pierce may or may not be a true number one, but his importance to the Colts is real. Occupying a corner and safety deep while providing an option to pick up huge yards in a hurry is something the Colts can’t replicate without him. He was supposed to be the guy. Missing time this year doesn’t mean he can’t be going forward, but being without him means the offense, Daniel Jones very much included, is going to feel the effects.
author: Jon Spradley

title: Colts sign veteran pass rusher Carl Lawson to practice squad
summary: The Colts added some veteran help to their defensive front Wednesday, signing defensive end Carl Lawson to the practice squad. Indianapolis also released tight end Kenny Fletcher Jr. from the practice squad to make room for Lawson, who had previously worked out for the Colts on Sept. 23. The timing is pretty easy to understand. […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TX - DECEMBER 22: Carl Lawson #55 of the Dallas Cowboys looks on from the field after an NFL football game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at AT&T Stadium on December 22, 2024 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Colts added some veteran help to their defensive front Wednesday, signing defensive end Carl Lawson to the practice squad. Indianapolis also released tight end Kenny Fletcher Jr. from the practice squad to make room for Lawson, who had previously worked out for the Colts on Sept. 23. The timing is pretty easy to understand. Arden Key is expected to miss time with an injury, while Micheal Clemons is already on injured reserve, leaving the Colts thinner than they would like at defensive end. Lawson gives them an experienced option who already has familiarity with defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo’s system. Lawson played under Anarumo in Cincinnati during the 2019 and 2020 seasons, and 2020 was arguably the best year of his career. He recorded 64 pressures that season and continued to establish himself as a disruptive rotational pass rusher. That familiarity should help if Indianapolis eventually needs to elevate him to the active roster. The 31-year-old has played eight NFL seasons with the Bengals, Jets, Cowboys and Ravens, appearing in 90 games with 34 starts. Over that span, he has recorded 32 sacks, 122 quarterback hits, 32 tackles for loss and four forced fumbles. His role has decreased in recent years, though, and he played just 26 defensive snaps for Baltimore last season. This should not be viewed as some major solution to the Colts’ pass-rush problems. Lawson is being added to the practice squad in October for a reason, and expecting him to suddenly become the player he was several years ago would be unrealistic. Still, the move makes sense considering the state of the defensive line. Indianapolis enters its Week 5 matchup against Pittsburgh ranked 31st in total defense, allowing 423.8 yards per game. The Colts have struggled to consistently affect opposing quarterbacks, and injuries have now taken away two veterans from an edge group that was already short on proven difference-makers. Lawson at least gives Anarumo another player he knows and trusts, along with someone who has shown in the past that he can create pressure when used in the right role. If Key remains out for multiple games, it would not be surprising to see Lawson elevated and given rotational snaps sooner rather than later. For now, he gives the Colts some needed insurance at a position that has quickly become even thinner.
author: Andrew Aziz

title: Where’s CJ Allen?
summary: The Colts used their first pick of the 2026 NFL Draft on CJ Allen because they believed he could play early. Chris Ballard called him an athletic, fast MIKE and said Allen would be a “green-dot guy for us from the get-go.” Indianapolis liked him enough at No. 53 overall that Ballard considered trading down […]
full_text: WESTFIELD, IN - AUGUST 20: Indianapolis Colts linebacker CJ Allen (53) runs through a drill during the Indianapolis Colts and Atlanta Falcons joint training camp practice on August 20, 2026 at the Grand Park Sports Campus in Westfield, IN. (Photo by Zach Bolinger/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Colts used their first pick of the 2026 NFL Draft on CJ Allen because they believed he could play early. Chris Ballard called him an athletic, fast MIKE and said Allen would be a “green-dot guy for us from the get-go.” Indianapolis liked him enough at No. 53 overall that Ballard considered trading down again and decided against it because the Colts did not want to risk losing him. Four games into his NFL career, Allen has played 11 defensive snaps. He played zero against Washington. That needs an explanation. Akeem Davis-Gaither played 62 of the Colts’ 64 defensive snaps Sunday. Jaylon Carlies played 30, Bryce Boettcher played 18 and Austin Ajiake played 17. Allen, the first player Indianapolis drafted five months ago, never got on the field defensively. So, where is CJ Allen? The Colts have boxed him into one position Lou Anarumo was asked about Allen’s lack of playing time Monday, and his answer gave us a pretty clear idea of how the Colts currently view their linebacker room. “Two totally different positions… Austin went out there in a pass situation, we were anticipating a certain thing and he plays DIME and CJ plays backer. Akeem is playing well and we were playing well. CJ is getting better each week in practice and he will get his opportunities in practice. Play count was low at one point so no need to rest Akeem, but not down on CJ. Not down on CJ, he’s working his tail off and he’ll have his opportunities.” Technically, that explanation makes sense. Davis-Gaither is playing MIKE and wearing the green dot. Carlies, Boettcher and Ajiake are being used in different roles, primarily at WILL or in sub-packages. Allen is currently being treated as the direct backup to Davis-Gaither, so Ajiake getting 17 snaps does not necessarily mean the coaching staff thinks Ajiake is a better linebacker than Allen. The problem is the Colts created that problem themselves. If Allen is only going to play MIKE, and Davis-Gaither is going to play 62 of 64 snaps whenever he is healthy, then when exactly is Allen supposed to play? You have essentially taken your top draft pick and placed him behind one of the few defenders on the roster who almost never leaves the field. That makes no sense to me. Davis-Gaither has played better over the last couple of games, and because he has the green dot, he naturally needs to be on the field more than most linebackers. Fine, but he also was not particularly good during the first couple weeks of the season, and nothing he has done should make the Colts terrified of taking him off the field for a handful of snaps. Allen does not need to replace him, but he needs to play. Allen is not a raw developmental linebacker Allen’s background makes the situation even harder to understand. He started at Georgia as a freshman and eventually became a First-Team All-American. He played three seasons in Kirby Smart’s defense and was the green-dot linebacker for a program that has produced Roquan Smith, Quay Walker, Nakobe Dean and a ridiculous number of NFL defenders. Colts linebackers coach James Bettcher specifically praised Allen’s communication and football intelligence before the season, noting that he was constantly making coverage checks and adjusting the front at Georgia. This is not a converted safety trying to learn linebacker and this is not a small-school prospect who spent Saturdays playing against guys who are now selling insurance. Allen played linebacker in one of the best and most complicated defenses in college football. Indianapolis drafted him in the second round in large part because the team believed his intelligence would allow him to transition quickly. Now we are being told he essentially has to wait behind Davis-Gaither because he is a MIKE. Allen did miss roughly a month of training camp, and that deserves to be mentioned. Missing that much time as a rookie absolutely hurts development, especially in a new defense. I would understand if he were behind where the Colts originally expected him to be, but we are also four regular-season games into the season now, not two days removed from his return. At some point, practice has to turn into playing. There is a difference between sitting and developing I am probably more sympathetic than most people when teams choose not to immediately throw young players onto the field. I argued for patience with Anthony Richardson when almost everyone wanted him starting immediately. Quarterback is difficult, and putting a young player on the field before he understands what he is seeing can do more harm than good. There are plenty of positions where sitting, watching and learning can be extremely beneficial. Linebacker is also much easier to rotate than quarterback. Nobody is asking the Colts to bench Davis-Gaither and give Allen 64 snaps next week. Get him eight. Then 12. Then 15. Give him a series at MIKE. Put him at WILL in another package. Let him cover. Let him play downhill against the run. Find out what translates and what does not. There is a huge difference between protecting a young player and burying him and right now, Allen is being buried. Boettcher has already played 79 defensive snaps this season. Allen has played 11. There is no reasonable argument that the talent difference between those two players should result in that kind of gap. And if Davis-Gaither is apparently playing too well to come off the field, then stop treating Allen as a MIKE-only linebacker. Why can’t he play WILL? This is the part of Anarumo’s explanation that bothers me the most. Why are the Colts rotating three different players through the WILL spot while keeping Allen glued to the bench as Davis-Gaither’s backup? Carlies is the obvious player whose snaps should be available. He played 42 defensive snaps against Baltimore earlier this season and did not record a single statistic. Not one!! His interception against Washington was a nice play, but one interception does not erase years of very little production. If the choice is between continuing to give Carlies 25-30 snaps a game or using some of those snaps to develop the player you just selected 53rd overall, I know which direction I am going. Allen has enough athleticism to run and cover. His college tape showed a player comfortable operating in space as well as inside the box. Nothing about his profile suggested a linebacker who could only stand in the middle of the defense and call plays. If Anarumo wants Davis-Gaither at MIKE because of the green dot, then work Allen in elsewhere. That is coaching! The answer cannot simply be, “They play different positions,” as if those positions were assigned at birth. Other rookie linebackers are already producing The rest of the 2026 linebacker class also makes Allen’s usage look strange. Jacob Rodriguez, who went 43rd overall to Miami, was one of my favourite prospects in the entire draft. Through three games he already had 28 tackles and an interception and had taken over defensive communication duties for the Dolphins. He is now the betting favourite for Defensive Rookie of the Year at +300. Anthony Hill Jr. went seven picks after Allen at No. 60 overall. He immediately won a starting job with Tennessee, recorded 34 tackles in his first three games and was named NFL Defensive Rookie of the Month for September. Sonny Styles was obviously drafted much earlier at No. 7 overall, so the expectations are different, but he has already become an important part of Washington’s defense. He has started all four games, played more than 200 snaps, intercepted a pass, forced a fumble and earned NFC Defensive Player of the Week honors. Every prospect develops differently, so this is not…

title: Colts’ Week 4 QB Analysis: What was that?!
summary: Thanks to the nflFastR project, Pro Football Focus for the timely sources of data. For those of you new to this, I will publish key QB stats each week judging how well the Colts’ QB performed. Yes, O-Line, receivers, and play-calling impact these numbers but they are primarily QB measures. I will probably modify the charts throughout the season. […]
full_text: Thanks to the nflFastR project, Pro Football Focus for the timely sources of data. For those of you new to this, I will publish key QB stats each week judging how well the Colts’ QB performed. Yes, O-Line, receivers, and play-calling impact these numbers but they are primarily QB measures. I will probably modify the charts throughout the season. Commentary will be brief but feel free to let me know in the comments that stats aren’t everything. (click charts for larger view) That first quarter—and most of the second—may very well have been the worst performance I’ve ever seen from a starting quarterback. Jones improved as the game went on, but not nearly enough to climb out of the bottom tier of quarterbacks in Week 4. HOW WELL? mouseover definitions: arsr , edp , sg% , oz% , pr% , tip , ttt , adot , ay/c , yac , yacoe , yd/c , ac% , cpoe , aypa , drp , scr% , ta% , sck% , aa% , ny/d , ny/p , 1st% , td% , to% , qbsr , epa/p , adj/p Indianapolis got excellent production from its running game while leaning towards the pass on early downs. (2nd ARSR; 13th EDP) Jones faced about an average amount of pressure, but only because he got the ball out very quickly, which means the O-line really let him down this week. (17th PR%; 30th TIP; 29th TTT) He had the shortest attempts in the league (3.8 yards), and even his completions produced very little yardage either through the air or after the catch. (32nd ADOT; 28th AY/C; 22nd YAC; 32nd YD/C) His 67.9% adjusted completion rate may sound good but given the depth of throws it was lower than expected. Combine that with the poor yards after the catch and he was near the bottom of the league in production per attempt. (20th AC%; 26th CPOE; 30th AYPA) Jones didn’t scramble at all, but he had to throw the ball away five times so maybe we should be glad he only had an average sack rate ( 28th SCR%; 1st TA%; 16th SCK%) Once all of those abandoned plays were incorporated, the passing game produced almost nothing on a play-by-play basis. (31st NY/D; 31st NY/P) Jones could not move the chains so its no surprise that he ended with just a single touchdown (29th 1ST%; 20th TD%) Turnovers were again another major problem. Jones threw an interception and lost a fumble off a sack giving him one of the highest turnover rates this week. (4th TO%) Overall, this wasn’t just a couple of disastrous plays dragging down an otherwise decent game. Jones produced a successful play on only 34% of his QB plays , while the sack-fumble and interception added two particularly costly negatives. He finished near the bottom of the league in both consistency and overall value. (29th QBSR; 28th EPA/P) mouseover definitions: ay< , dp% , ay/c , yac , yd/c , ac% , aypa , drp% , aypa , ta% , ypa , sck% , ny/a , scr% , ny/d , car% , ny/p , 1st% , any/p , td% , any/p , to% , any/p , epa/p , opd , adj/p Jones simply didn’t generate enough through the air. The short passing game produced very little yardage, and below-average completion production pushed the offense even farther down. The only way to make that situation work is to boost first downs by avoiding sacks and turnovers, but that didn’t happen happen. Jones had a brutal start, producing only one positive value play in the first fourteen, including two turnovers . It was near the end of the 2nd quarter before he started digging himself out of the hole and if we only look at that point forward, then he had a decent game. But the first half counts and his numbers never recovered from how poorly he started the game. Jones’ season is moving in the wrong direction. After a poor Week 1, he rebounded in Week 2, but that improvement didn’t last—falling sharply since then. All four measures are now trending downward, with both his consistency and overall production deteriorating. HOW FAR? The slow start really stands out here as well. Jones completed some passes early, but almost everything was underneath and produced very little. He eventually found a little more downfield production, but never established a long sustained rhythm that might have saved an overall ineffective passing day. Jones went extremely short in Week 4, with both his target depth and the depth of his completions falling off a cliff. More importantly, this wasn’t just a one-week blip—the recent trend has been steadily toward a shorter passing game. I’m going to leave the same comment I did last week: Jones passing short is fine, but not making up for it with YAC and a high completion rate is not. TO WHO? Laquon Treadwell led Indianapolis with 42 receiving yards (if you can call that leading), with Tyler Warren right behind him at 41 receiving yards. Downs leads the team in receiving yards, with Warren and Treadwell fairly close behind. Warren has generated much of his production after the catch, while Treadwell’s yardage has come more from deeper completions. Most of Jones’ receivers produced below-average value per target in Week 4, and most of that production also came on shorter throws—clustering them in the quadrant I like to call, “the worst quadrant”. Season-wise, the numbers spread out about how you would expect although I would really like the Colts to get more high value passes to Warren. HOW ACCURATE? Jones posted an average completion rate, but with such a short average depth of target, he should have been completing passes at a much higher rate—indicating another below-average week for accuracy. HOW FAST? Jones’ time to throw was the quickest it’s been over the last 18 weeks, largely because the pressure forced him to get the ball out quickly. Even with an extremely short passing game, he is still releasing the ball much faster than expected for the depth of his throws. I’d like to say that is because he is processing the game quickly, but its more because he is forced to. TO WHERE? Jones struggled on both the short throws under 10 yards and the deep passes beyond 20, but he found some success in the intermediate 10-to-20-yard range. Maybe by the end of the year, there will be more green.

On Wednesday, punter Matt Araiza represented the unit’s performance when he earned an accolade from the NFL. Araiza was named AFC Special Teams Player of […]
full_text: (Photo by Chris Unger/Getty Images) | Getty Images Kansas City Chiefs head coach Andy Reid called the special teams the best phase among the three in the team’s 30-27 win over the Las Vegas Raiders in Week 4. On Wednesday, punter Matt Araiza represented the unit’s performance when he earned an accolade from the NFL. An extra special game🦵 Congratulations to @matt_araiza ! pic.twitter.com/8YwGnH6b34 — Kansas City Chiefs (@Chiefs) October 7, 2026 Araiza was named AFC Special Teams Player of the Week. As the Chiefs noted in a Twitter post, Araiza had five (out of five) punts land inside the 20-yard line, including a late-game punt downed at the one-yard line by rookie safety Xavier Nwankpa, with help from rookie running back Emmett Johnson. Interesting rewatching the Chiefs' fake punt. Cochrane (43) and Christiansen (48) seemed to be part of a check with their hand signals. Jaden Hicks (21) was also wide open for a pass if Matt Araiza wanted to try his hand there. pic.twitter.com/S296qO0gdg — Jesse Newell (@jessenewell) October 5, 2026 He also executed the fake punt perfectly, not overthinking it by trying to pass to safety Jaden Hicks out on a route, as Jesse Newell of The Athletic pointed out on Twitter . Through four games, Araiza leads all NFL punters in yards per punt (52.3) and has allowed the seventh-fewest return yards (40). He also has the highest rate of punts that land inside the 20-yard line (75%); 9 of his 12 punts have pinned the opponent more than 80 yards away from the end zone. Four punters have launched a longer punt than Araiza this year, but the long of 69 yards is still a top-5 mark. Araiza has been one of the team’s most underrated difference makers in the 4-0 start to the season.

title: Chiefs Rookie Report: Grading Kahlil Benson through four games
summary: The Kansas City Chiefs head into their bye week with a perfect 4-0 record. A tight win in Las Vegas on Sunday helped the Chiefs remain unbeaten and put them at the top of the AFC and the AFC West. Many players have stood out this season, but rookie offensive lineman Kahlil Benson has played […]
full_text: (Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Kansas City Chiefs head into their bye week with a perfect 4-0 record. A tight win in Las Vegas on Sunday helped the Chiefs remain unbeaten and put them at the top of the AFC and the AFC West. Many players have stood out this season, but rookie offensive lineman Kahlil Benson has played one of the most important roles on the team. A training camp standout, Benson seemed poised to compete for the starting right tackle job, but with returning starter Josh Simmons out, Benson started every game at left tackle to begin the 2026 season. In a move not often seen, the Chiefs brain trust has felt confident enough to line up Benson as Patrick Mahomes’ blind-side protector after Mahomes came off a serious knee injury. So far this season, the Chiefs have one of the NFL’s most potent offenses, and while the team has helped Benson, he’s reciprocated and put together solid tape. Grad ing Benson For game grades, I broke them into three categories to create an overall grade. My criteria were run blocking, true pass protection, and assisted pass protection. Run blocking is as black and white as it can be, but to keep his pass-blocking grade from getting oversaturated, I included true pass protection, which is traditional drop-back passes or plays where Benson is in a classic pass-blocking set. Assisted is where I included plays like RPO’s, screens, play-action looks, and other plays that can give offensive linemen easy plays to win. The Chiefs have used plenty of these, but the true pass-blocking grade tells us whether Benson has what it takes to keep playing the position in the NFL. Through four weeks—against formidable pass rushers—Benson has graded a 74% for true pass protection , with an assisted pass protection grade of 85%. His run game has been good as well, with a 74% grade as a run blocker . Overall, this puts his season grade at a 77% The team has definitely played to his strengths as a player with quicker passing patterns and an uptick in running the football, but Benson has delivered for what he has been asked to do this season. Pass protection Benson has been solid in pass protection so far this season and has yet to allow a sack. This has been largely because the Chiefs have emphasized getting the ball out of Mahomes’ hands more quickly. In 2023, Mahomes averaged 2.5 seconds of pocket time per throw, the seventh-longest in the NFL. Three seasons later, Mahomes is at 2.2 seconds of pocket time and below the league average. It has taken the Chiefs some time to get here, but the emphasis on a quick passing game has helped players like Benson, who rely on physicality. Benson wants to win snaps quickly; this is where he can put his power on full display. In his first game, he faced one of the NFL’s best edge rushers, Nik Bonitto. Bonitto relies on speed and bend and looks to rush wide. Benson is patient out of his stance, and quarterback Patrick Mahomes is only taking a three-step drop, so Benson knows he can run Bonitto wide if needed. As the two meet, Benson fires a big shot and blasts Bonitto upfield, finishing him to the ground. The clean pocket allows Mahomes ample time to run and pick up yards with his legs. Benson can have issues with quickness at times, but when he gets his hands on a defender, he ends snaps quickly with powerful grip strength and a strong base. A few snaps a game, Benson shows his pass-protection deficiencies. Knowing he has issues with the speed of the game—many undrafted rookies do—the Chiefs have been careful to give him help when needed, but one inconsistent area is his striking and hand placement. Solid out of his stance, Benson goes wide with his hands and gives up his chest to the edge rusher. He can’t recover and ends up on the ground as Mahomes is hit. Benson’s pass blocking is still a work in progress, but with the new-look Chiefs offense, his strengths are maximized, and much of this starts with the run game. Run blocking Running back Kenneth Walker has run wild this season, and Benson has been instrumental in this with his blocking. Benson’s strength and power translate well to the new run game, and so far he has delivered. While his technique still needs refining, he plays with a nasty streak and can move a man off a spot, opening lanes for his running back. His background as a guard during his underclassman years in college helps him create leverage from his stance and drives his feet through contact. Sealing the backside of the zone has become extremely important with Walker running the ball, given his vision and cutting ability. Backs with patience require offensive lines that give tremendous effort, play in and play out. The bottom line The Chiefs have tried to play young tackles with varying degrees of success, but this has culminated in finding a solid player in Benson. Perfect? No, but far from bad. Benson has benefited from a Chiefs team that is running the ball at the same rate they once did with greats like Priest Holmes and Jamaal Charles, and is helping Kenneth Walker to what could be a remarkable season. Benson might not be the left tackle of the future, but he has a bright future with the team, at either guard or tackle. Brute strength, physicality, and maximum effort can mask weaknesses, and Benson grades highly in all three.
author: Caleb James

title: Chiefs Mailbag: How could the Chiefs address wide receiver?
summary: Welcome back to the Arrowhead Pride Mailbag! Throughout the season, keep watching The Feed for an opportunity to submit your questions about the Kansas City Chiefs! The Chiefs will enjoy some early time off with a Week 5 bye after going to 4-0 with a 30-27 defeat of the Las Vegas Raiders. Let’s see what […]
full_text: (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome back to the Arrowhead Pride Mailbag ! Throughout the season, keep watching The Feed for an opportunity to submit your questions about the Kansas City Chiefs ! The Chiefs will enjoy some early time off with a Week 5 bye after going to 4-0 with a 30-27 defeat of the Las Vegas Raiders . Let’s see what questions (about wide receivers and other topics) are on our readers’ minds. Andyreidsmustache_ asks: Rashee Rice has a hamstring injury, and Tyquan Thornton is out for, at minimum, a significant portion of the year if not the entirety of it. Who are some possibilities at WR available, and more importantly, who would we realistically be able to get from a salary cap and scheme fit? The big unknown right now is Rice’s status. There does not seem to be significant concern that his hamstring injury is a long-term problem. By some accounts, Rice could even suit up in Week 6 against the Los Angeles Chargers . A heavily rumored wideout addition will be covered in the next question, but the initial focus should be on Rice given how much of the offense runs through him. If his hamstring is unlikely to stretch into a month-long absence, the Chiefs would do well to get a serious look at Jalen Royals and Cyrus Allen. Neither looked great in brief moments against the Raiders, but the sample is too small to draw real conclusions. With Rice headed for free agency after the season, Kansas City should want to know more about how the pair perform. A couple of interesting low-cost options are Cedric Tillman — currently on the New Orleans Saints’ practice squad — and current Cleveland Browns afterthought Jerry Jeudy. Both played for Chiefs wide receivers coach Chad O’Shea in Cleveland. Tillman could be signed outright to a minimum salary. Jeudy would come with a very affordable salary in a trade, and the Browns likely would prefer to cut ties with Jeudy sooner rather than later. If Rice is available, however, it’s hard to see a path to either having a major role. Arizona Cardinals wideout Marvin Harrison Jr. has not lived up to his lofty draft status and seems a good bet to be traded soon. Harrison would come with an affordable 2027 salary. However, the Cardinals will likely drive a hard bargain to recoup the value spent to draft Harrison in 2024. He also has some of the limitations that sometimes leave Chiefs fans frustrated with Rice. Thornton himself seemed an irredeemable bust after washing out with the New England Patriots . I would be interested in seeking Kansas City look at a similarly profiled player in former third-round selection Jalin Hyatt, currently on the New York Giants ’ practice squad. At any rate, I expect preseason favorite Andrew Armstrong to get called up to help at wide receiver in at least one of the Chiefs’ upcoming games. Kansas City bringing back a player like Justin Watson or Mecole Hardman to the practice squad would also hardly be surprising. JoBackson asks: Where will KC find the money to pay Cheetah? At this point, it would be an upset if former Chiefs wideout Tyreek Hill — apparently in the final stages of recovering from a gruesome knee injury — does not return to Kansas City. I fully expect that to happen within the next few weeks. Hill forced a trade out of Kansas City to receive a monstrous $120 million extension from the Miami Dolphins in 2022. I don’t think anyone expects him to command even average wide receiver money on an in-season contract after multiple surgeries. In four games last season, Hill caught only 21 passes for 265 yards and a single touchdown. Whatever contract he signs will likely be built around a guaranteed minimum base salary (prorated for the weeks he signs for) plus incentives. Given his low stats from a year ago, it would be really easy to build easily attainable incentives that would be categorized as Not Likely to be Earned for cap purposes. My biggest question about Hill’s signing is whether he will be willing to accept a practice squad contract initially to acclimate his body to football activities while waiting to make his actual debut. KCMagic asks: Is it time to bring back running back Kareem Hunt and see if he has anything left in the tank. Bye week is perfect time. It’s now a trend (3 straight games) where the Chiefs have failed to run for 1-2 yards on third and fourth downs. I think the Chiefs need to try to find new things to do with the current room. Yes, it has been frustrating to see the Chiefs stopped short multiple times, and Hunt was automatic last year. But it is also hard to fit another running back on the team, from the standpoint of both the 53-man roster and the 48 players who dress for game day. It is really hard to have a player designated for one job who rarely will call for more than four or five snaps per game. It is even harder when that hypothetical player would offer no value on special teams. Third-string running back Brashard Smith hasn’t moved the needle much on either offense or special teams. However, with Thornton out and Hill probably a month away from contributing if he returns, Smith is the only real option on the Chiefs’ roster to add speed on offense. Papajazz asks: Did the Raiders show some of the better teams how to beat us? The blueprint to beat the Chiefs has long been to get pressure with four defensive linemen and stack coverage on the back end. Kenneth Walker has largely made that plan obsolete. The Raiders exploited some things in the Chiefs’ defense that were concerns entering the game. I do think some of the issues we are seeing will improve as the unit gets more experience playing together. How much it improves will likely determine Kansas City’s ultimate 2026 ceiling. I hope the Chiefs have learned the dangers of beating themselves, especially on defense (and frustratingly on special teams). The defense missed chances to get off the field on third down before two Raiders field goals, although one likely still would have resulted in a successful try. Both drives were kept alive by penalties on cornerback Nohl Williams. Another Las Vegas field goal came after only a 19-yard drive that started inside Kansas City territory because of a long kickoff return. At least six points for the Raiders probably come off the board without self-inflicted Chiefs blunders. GoChiefs70 asks: This is a question pertaining to the questionable call in last night‘s game at the end where it looked like the ball hit the ground on that very last Raider drive. They rushed up and spiked it, so I guess it could not be reviewed at that point. If Andy Reid had thrown a red flag before the ball was spiked, would it have been eligible to review? Shockingly, the NFL finds new ways for officiating controversy to arise each and every week. The Chiefs were trapped by the NFL’s own rules, as coaches can’t challenge in the last two minutes of a half. Even though the most severe of ophthalmology patients could see that Raiders wideout Tre Tucker did not actually catch the ball, Kirk Cousins spiking the ball counted as a play, and the window to review the pass to Tucker expired. Obviously, the league avoided an embarrassing scenario since Kansas City won. If the league had gone ahead and contradicted its own rules by reviewing the play after the first-down spike, we would never have heard the end of how they bailed out the Chiefs. The best solution would be to make a rule that spiking the ball doesn’t count for replay rules and to give the league until an actual play is run to initiate a review. Given how rare this situation seems, I doubt fixing it will be a high offseason priority. If Reid or any coach faces such a scenario going forward, they should throw the red flag at the nearest official and get onto the field even though they aren’t allowed to. Give the league extra time to start the review process, and if the coach is ultimately fined, that is just part of the job. Thank you for reading this week’s Arrowhead Pride Mailbag ! We will…

title: NFL Power Rankings Week 5 Roundup: Chiefs strengthen spot near top
summary: The 2026 NFL regular season’s Week 4 featured the Kansas City Chiefs beating the Las Vegas Raiders, moving to 4-0, one of three NFL teams with that record. Let’s see how the national media responds in this week’s sampling of power rankings: NFL.com: 2 (No change) The average fan might view Sunday’s four-quarter battle with […]
full_text: (Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 2026 NFL regular season’s Week 4 featured the Kansas City Chiefs beating the Las Vegas Raiders , moving to 4-0, one of three NFL teams with that record. Let’s see how the national media responds in this week’s sampling of power rankings: NFL.com : 2 (No change) The average fan might view Sunday’s four-quarter battle with the Raiders as a red mark on Kansas City’s résumé. Not me. Las Vegas is scrappy and worthy of respect. Lesser teams would have crumbled in the desert. The Chiefs did the opposite, delivering timely, game-altering plays in the fourth quarter and holding on for a win made possible by the strength of their balanced, dynamic offense. ESPN : 2 (Up from 3) Four words to describe the first four weeks: In Walker we trust. Coach Andy Reid and offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy have no excuses to ever abandon the running game as long as running back Kenneth Walker III is healthy and on the field. Walker has completely transformed the Chiefs’ offense, allowing quarterback Patrick Mahomes to make more deep completions. Walker leads the NFL with 537 rushing yards and the team with six total touchdowns. The Chiefs should continue to rely on Walker following the bye week after injuries to receivers Tyquan Thornton (dislocated left ankle) and Rashee Rice (right hamstring). — Nate Taylor The Athletic : 2 (Up from 3) Concern level: None, now that they have Kenneth Walker After years of struggling to run the ball efficiently, the Chiefs gave Walker, the reigning Super Bowl MVP, a contract worth more than $14 million a season. So far, it’s looking like an incredible deal. Walker joined Billy Sims (from 1980) as the only NFL players in league history with at least 175 yards from scrimmage in three of their first four games with a new team. — Chad Graff and Josh Kendall Pro Football Talk : 2 (No change) They need help at receiver, badly. — Mike Florio CBSSports.com : 2 (Up from 3) They are 4-0, but they suffered some hits to the receiver position Sunday which are concerning. They have to reach out to Tyreek Hill. When will he be ready? — Pete Prisco Yahoo! Sports : 4 (Up from 3) If you want the Chiefs to fall off sometime soon, it’s probably not going to happen. Their upcoming schedule is soft and should lead to a start of 8-2 or better: Week 5: bye Week 6: vs. Chargers Week 7: at Seahawks Week 8: at Broncos Week 9: vs. Jets Week 10: at Falcons Week 11: vs. Cardinals That’s four games in which Kansas City should be significant favorites, and while the game at the Seahawks will be very tough, it’s not like the Broncos are playing great. That’s a winnable road game. A 4-2 run through those six games seems to be the worst outcome. The Chiefs aren’t going away. — Frank Schwab USA Today : 2 (No change) Will the AFC’s final undefeated team have anyone left to play wide receiver on the other side of their Week 5 bye after losing Rashee Rice and Tyquan Thornton in Vegas on Sunday? Maybe an old friend? — Nate Davis Sports Illustrated : 3 (No change) One of the most frustrating aspects of the Chiefs’ early-season run is that, for a decade, we wondered when this team was going to find quality edge rushing talent in the late rounds and a downhill running back that could transform the scheme. And just when we became positive the franchise was rebuilding, they came up with R Mason Thomas and Kenneth Walker III in one offseason. — Conor Orr FOX Sports : 2 (Up from 4) Their dismantling of the Broncos in Week 1 was a signal to the world that they were back, and they haven’t really stopped rolling since. Patrick Mahomes is looking like his old MVP self, at least as a passer, and it’s impossible to overstate what the addition of RB Kenneth Walker III, the NFL’s leading rusher, has done to their offense. They could use a little more of a pass rush to balance things out, but I trust Steve Spagnuolo to find that during this bye week. Stat To Know : Through their first 151 career starts (regular season and playoffs combined), Patrick Mahomes and Tom Brady now have identical 116-35 overall records. — Ralph Vacchiano

title: The good and the bad about the Chiefs’ win against the Raiders
summary: That was a great football game. The Kansas City Chiefs and the Las Vegas Raiders have often been a lopsided rivalry for the Chiefs, but the Raiders came into this game 3-0 and wanted to prove themselves. And to their credit, they showed up and competed. This game was a haymaker, with both sides having […]
full_text: (Photo by Steve Marcus/Getty Images) | Getty Images That was a great football game. The Kansas City Chiefs and the Las Vegas Raiders have often been a lopsided rivalry for the Chiefs, but the Raiders came into this game 3-0 and wanted to prove themselves. And to their credit, they showed up and competed. This game was a haymaker, with both sides having impressive moments, and the Chiefs ultimately made the timely plays to close it out. There’s a lot to be impressed with in this game, but let’s focus on two players that set the tone defensively: George Karlaftis’s impressive performance Kirk Cousins wasn’t sacked in this game, which might lead you to think the Chiefs’ defensive line didn’t get much pressure. However, the Chiefs did get pressure on Cousins in this game 34.6% of his dropbacks, which was 16th in the NFL for Week 4 . Without blitzes, the Chiefs were 12th at 34.2%. Two players led the charge in getting pressure in this game: defensive ends R Mason Thomas and George Karlaftis. Thomas finished the day with eight pressures, including five in the fourth quarter. Thomas took time to get into this game, but his speed and explosiveness off the edge showed up when it mattered. But for me, the most impressive performance for the Chiefs defense was Karlaftis. Karlaftis brought it all four quarters and did it on a higher snap count against the Raiders’ better tackle, left tackle Kolton Miller. Karlaftis isn’t always the most reliable pass rusher turning the corner, but he did it in this game. Here, he uses his hands to swipe down the tackle’s outside arm, then uses his speed to turn the corner and nearly get to the quarterback before he checks it down. Karlaftis establishing himself as a cornering threat opened up other pass rush moves, including this speed-to-power bull rush. Karlaftis flies off the ball and flashes that he’s trying to get upfield, which gets the tackle to subtly open his hip upfield. Karlaftis then turns toward the quarterback and attacks the tackle’s inside foot, which isn’t planted. Without that anchor foot established, it’s an easy run through for Karlaftis to get the pressure. Karlaftis did a very good job in this game, continuing to work late into the down to get off tackles, particularly going inside. His balance and torque were impressive. He got Miller to lean his upper body forward, which put him in a bad position to recover. Karlaftis could then work inside, using his inside hand to attack Miller’s inside shoulder and create separation. He did this 3-4 times this game, and it worked. Mansoor Delane’s impact as a run defender Mansoor Delane has been impressive as a rookie in many departments. He’s looked good in man coverage for the most part, sticking to receivers. When the Chiefs play zone coverage, Delane shows off impressive click-and-close and route recognition. However, what’s impressed me most about Delane so far is his play as a run defender. Delane has racked up 10 tackles in two straight games, and a lot of those plays are run stops. For a sub-190-pound player, that is impressive. The Raiders often ran condensed formations, which force corners into the run fit. They run a short-side toss here with the WR responsible to crack Delane. Delane sees this and gets outside the block, forces Ashton Jeanty back inside, and makes an impressive one-on-one tackle. Another short-side toss here, but Delane is now the furthest player to the edge, responsible for setting it. Delane strings out the run and keeps the running back from getting the angle on the sideline. If he can’t set an edge there, the running back beats Nick Bolton to the edge and that turns into a chunk run. This was a massive run stop by Delane that saved at least an explosive run, if not a house call. The Raiders call a counter play, shifting their third tight end and pulling their right guard. Tranquill flies too far upfield, Bolton gets caught, and Chamarri Conner gets pinned and falls over. Delane is the only free defender near the line of scrimmage. If he misses this tackle, the only guy left is Alohi Gilman one-on-one with a two-way go. Delane makes an incredibly clutch tackle that prevents an explosive run. The third-and-eight play call to end the game For the most part, I thought the Chiefs played and executed a fairly clean game, but what bothered me most was Andy Reid’s decision to pass on third and eight on the Chiefs’ last offensive drive. The Raiders had no timeouts with around ninety seconds left. If the Chiefs had run the ball, they would’ve been able to get the clock down to around 35-40 seconds. Instead, by throwing the ball and having it go incomplete, the Chiefs gave the Raiders a free forty seconds. To be fair to Reid, Matt Araiza had a great punt to get the Raiders downed at the 1, and Araiza had a great game punting even before that. Realistically, your defense should be able to get a stop there, which they did. However, the Raiders were knocking on field goal range with no timeouts. The Raiders offense played decently throughout the game, but they struggled to push the ball downfield, especially when forced to do it in obvious passing situations. If they had 40 fewer seconds to run their last drive, I just don’t think they could’ve picked up enough yards in time to get close. If this was a big playoff game against an elite quarterback, I totally understand giving Mahomes the ball to close the game, but in that specific context, you have to keep the clock running. Credit Araiza for the punt and the defense for coming through.

(Photo by Lee Coleman/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Chargers are adding another offensive lineman who has familiarity with offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel. On Tuesday, the Chargers announced the signing of former 49ers and Dolphins offensive tackle Daniel Brunskill to their practice squad. In a corresponding move, the Chargers are also releasing defensive tackle Jordan Jefferson. Along with the signing, the Chargers are also activating the 21-day practice windows for fullback Scott Matlock and offensive lineman Branson Taylor. Both players have been on IR since the preseason. we've signed T daniel brunskill to the practice squad + released DL jordan jefferson from the practice squad we also opened the practice windows for FB/DL scott matlock + G/T branson taylor pic.twitter.com/CmaErbX84s — Los Angeles Chargers (@chargers) October 6, 2026 Brunskill spent the first two seasons of his career with the Atlanta Falcons on their practice squad. In the spring of 2019, he also played one season in the now-defunct Alliance of American Football for the San Diego Fleet. From 2019 to 2022, Brunskill was a member of the San Francisco 49ers where he overlapped with McDaniel. He started 42 of 61 games for the Niners during that span, including 33 starts of a possible 34 during the 2020 and 2021 regular seasons. From 2023-2024, Brunskill started 24 of 31 games for the Titans. The 32-year old Brunskill was most recently with the Dolphins in 2025 where he started five games for McDaniel while playing in 16 total contests.
